art/art-history.1f49d966ca32: Street art and murals. Nineteen ninety, Berlin, Germany. Art leaves the museum. After the Berlin Wall fell, artists from around the world painted about one point three kilometers of it, about zero point eight miles — the East Side Gallery. Meanwhile in China: contemporary art was booming; Beijing’s seven nine eight Art District turned old factories into galleries in the early two thousands.
art/art-history.7f86474d4dce: Post-Impressionism. Eighteen eighty-nine, Saint-Rémy, France. Color and brushstroke show feeling, not just what the eye sees. Van Gogh’s sky swirls; Seurat built pictures from tiny dots, pointillism. Meanwhile in China: Ren Bonian and other Shanghai School painters mixed traditional ink painting with bright colors for city buyers.
art/art-history.92d8d9160538: Computed: forty thousand years ago equals midnight — the oldest known figurative cave paintings are at least this old; today equals twenty-four hundred, so one hour about one thousand six hundred sixty-seven years. art/art-history.36b3cf7ea471: Renaissance. about fifteen oh three to fifteen nineteen, Florence, Italy. Linear perspective and sfumato, “smoky”: no hard outlines, just soft glazes of oil paint so thin you can’t see brushstrokes. Meanwhile in China: the Ming dynasty — the Forbidden City was finished in fourteen twenty and Jingdezhen kilns were making blue-and-white porcelain.

art/art-history.3d9783c37813: Japanese woodblock prints. about eighteen thirty to eighteen thirty-two, Edo, Tokyo, Japan. Ukiyo-e prints: one carved wooden block per color, thousands of cheap copies. Hokusai used a new imported pigment — Prussian blue. Meanwhile in China: the Qing dynasty under the Daoguang Emperor; the Opium War would begin in eighteen forty.
art/art-history.6f75eeac9b8e: Song landscape painting. Eleven thirteen, Kaifeng, Northern Song China. Landscape becomes the hero. Eighteen-year-old Wang Ximeng painted mountains in brilliant mineral blue and green, from azurite and malachite, on a scroll almost twelve meters long, about thirty-nine feet. Meanwhile in Europe: Romanesque churches with thick walls and round arches; the Bayeux Tapestry told a story in embroidery. The tapestry dates to about the ten seventies.

art/art-history.bf4e65a9c75b: Seventeen thousand years ago someone crawled into a cave in France with a torch and painted a horse on the rock. Over two thousand years ago the Greeks built the Parthenon in marble; in eighteen eighty-nine Van Gogh painted a swirling night sky from his window. Today artists paint walls with spray cans. Art keeps changing — but why people make it never has.
art/art-history.cd577fb9a73b: Impressionism. Eighteen seventy-two, Le Havre, France. Paint outdoors, fast, in broken dabs of color to catch changing light. Paint in metal tubes made it easy. Paint in metal tubes was invented in eighteen forty-one. A critic mocked this painting’s title — and the name “Impressionism” stuck. Meanwhile in China: the Self-Strengthening Movement was building China’s first modern factories and shipyards. In Chinese, the movement is called 洋务运动.
art/art-history.42b289b168b8: Georges Seurat, A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, eighteen eighty-four to eighteen eighty-six, Art Institute of Chicago
art/art-history.a4e73731e2bf: Cave art. about seventeen thousand years ago, Lascaux, France. Paint from the earth: red and yellow ochre, black charcoal — dabbed with moss or blown through hollow bones. Bumps in the rock became the bellies of animals. Meanwhile in China: people in Xianrendong Cave, Jiangxi, were making some of the world’s oldest known pottery, around twenty thousand years ago.
art/art-history.7d6b2af82164: The real Lascaux cave has been closed to the public since nineteen sixty-three; visitors see replicas. Many Lascaux photos on Commons are of replicas — captions say so.

Kandinsky had started painting abstracts around nineteen ten to nineteen thirteen. Meanwhile in China: Xu Beihong, 徐悲鸿, combined Western drawing with Chinese ink — famous for his galloping horses.

We “see” it because gas pulled from its companion star heats up to millions of degrees and glows in X-rays. Event horizon equals the point of no return.

Example: M eight seven, a giant elliptical whose central black hole was the first ever photographed, twenty nineteen. Elliptical equals egg-shaped and old.

astronomy/kepler-laws.d48d47e7a9eb: Kepler’s third law. T squared equals a cubed, years and AU. Published in sixteen nineteen in Harmonices Mundi, “The Harmony of the World”. T is the orbital period in years; a is the semi-major axis, half the long axis, the “average” distance, in AU. For every planet, T squared is about a cubed. Example: Jupiter, a equals five point two AU: a cubed equals one hundred forty-one, so T equals the square root of one hundred forty-one, about eleven point nine years. Newton showed the full rule: T squared equals four pi squared a cubed divided by G M, where M is the mass of the central body. Measure a moon’s orbit and you can weigh its planet! Farther out, slower AND a longer path, a much longer year. The law uses a, the average distance, semi-major axis, not the starting distance. Launch from the same spot at different speeds and you get different a and different T.

astronomy/kepler-laws.315793af06d0: Hohmann transfer. The fuel-saving road between two orbits. Described by German engineer Walter Hohmann in nineteen twenty-five, decades before any spacecraft flew. The transfer orbit is an ellipse with perihelion at Earth’s orbit, one AU, and aphelion at Mars’s orbit, one point five two AU, so a equals one point two six AU. By Kepler’s third law its full period is one point two six to the power of one point five, about one point four two years; the probe flies half of it: about two hundred fifty-nine days, or eight point five months. Real missions often spend a bit more fuel to arrive sooner: Perseverance took about two hundred three days, launched July thirtieth, twenty twenty, landed February eighteenth, twenty twenty-one. Speed up at Earth, coast half an ellipse, speed up again at Mars. You don’t aim at where Mars is when you launch. You aim at where Mars WILL BE about eight point five months later.

astronomy/kepler-laws.5e1b3db9da6e: Common mix-up: There is plenty of gravity at the space station’s height: about eighty-nine percent of what you feel on the ground. Astronauts float because they are falling together with the station.
astronomy/kepler-laws.33218e067453: Supports GSE S six E one, especially element d: develop and use a model to explain how gravity and inertia govern the motion of objects in the solar system; the Mars mission also connects to S six E two, positions in the Earth-Moon-Sun system change over time in predictable ways.
astronomy/kepler-laws.faadb073f199: Semi-major axis a equals one point five two four astronomical units. Perihelion one point three eight astronomical units, aphelion one point six seven astronomical units: the far point is one point two one times the near point.

astronomy/measuring-distance.68827178c75f: For thousands of years nobody could detect a star’s parallax. In eighteen thirty-eight the German astronomer Friedrich Bessel finally measured about zero point three arcseconds for the star six one Cygni: the first time anyone knew the distance to a star.
astronomy/measuring-distance.496da16e138e: Suggested flow: do the thumb experiment as a whole class, then swap “two eyes” for Earth’s orbit in the three D model; read the parallax in the telescope view and compute distances; pair the inverse-square sim with a flashlight and graph paper; let students measure a Cepheid’s period, read the chart and compute the distance themselves; use Distance detective as an exit ticket.
astronomy/measuring-distance.83cef837bff3: ESA’s Gaia spacecraft launched in twenty thirteen and worked until twenty twenty-five at the L two point, one point five million kilometers from Earth. It measured parallaxes for about one point five billion stars, the best to about zero point zero zero zero zero two arcseconds: like seeing the width of a human hair from one thousand kilometers away, six hundred miles.
astronomy/measuring-distance.b7c73d2a0724: two parsecs, about six point five light-years
astronomy/measuring-distance.caefc0d0fbc3: Read the distance-ladder figure: which method reaches the Andromeda Galaxy, at two point five million light-years, but NOT parallax?
astronomy/measuring-distance.7f609843bf5f: Her twenty-five Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud are all at about the same distance, so “looks brighter” really means “is brighter”. The period-luminosity relation was born; today it is called the Leavitt law.
astronomy/measuring-distance.ae321ac1f1b8: Follow ten days up to the line, then across: between three thousand and ten thousand, about three thousand five hundred Suns.

astronomy/measuring-distance.16197a54ffbc: A star has a parallax of zero point five arcseconds. How far away is it?
astronomy/measuring-distance.8f04d95375fb: Baseline: Earth’s orbit: one astronomical unit equals one hundred fifty million kilometers. A longer baseline makes the same star shift more, easier to measure, but the distance you compute stays the same.
astronomy/measuring-distance.a99fe64d8d2e: Distance in light-years on a log scale: each big step is one thousand times the one before. Method ranges are approximate. Object distances: NASA and ESA Gaia values, rounded.
astronomy/measuring-distance.852a3c0f0ef2: Rung three, Redshift: reading stretched light
astronomy/measuring-distance.f342c9fa8db1: Turn the angle into “radians”: six point one degrees equals zero point one zero seven radians. Then six point four centimeters divided by zero point one zero seven, about sixty centimeters: exactly the thumb’s distance! Star parallax uses the same math.
astronomy/measuring-distance.8890cc96df36: Smaller parallax means farther away: ten parsecs versus one hundred parsecs.

Dots are placed using that relation, approximate; real stars scatter about plus or minus twenty percent around the line, shaded band.
astronomy/measuring-distance.77927d8ce0b8: Rung one, Parallax: try it with your thumb first

astronomy/measuring-distance.cf9abcb7b14e: A star whose parallax is exactly one arcsecond is one parsec away: about three point two six light-years or thirty-one trillion kilometers, nineteen trillion miles. Parallax zero point one arcseconds, ten parsecs.

astronomy/measuring-distance.44a9e0edcfe1: Beyond grade six: arcseconds and parsecs, the inverse-square law, log scales, spectra and redshift, Hubble’s law. astronomy/measuring-distance.98e71081da77: A circle has three hundred sixty degrees; one degree equals sixty arcminutes; one arcminute equals sixty arcseconds, double prime. astronomy/measuring-distance.7c8b9e454ae0: A star’s light spreads out in all directions. At twice the distance the same light covers two times two equals four squares, and your telescope only catches one of them, so the star looks one quarter as bright.
astronomy/measuring-distance.632cc4ba19b7: Read the period-luminosity chart: about how many Suns is a Cepheid with a ten-day period?
astronomy/measuring-distance.8594f65e30ba: Stars are so far away that the gap between your eyes is useless. Astronomers use Earth’s orbit as their “two eyes”: in January and July, Earth is on opposite sides of the Sun, about three hundred million kilometers apart. Drag the time bar and watch a nearby star shift against much more distant background stars.
astronomy/measuring-distance.001c6f2449c4: Leavitt found it in nineteen twelve using Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud. Hubble later used it.
astronomy/measuring-distance.d83b6b0ecf7c: Supports GSE S six E one: a, asking questions about how models of the universe and Earth’s place in it changed with new evidence, Hubble’s V one proving Andromeda is a separate galaxy is a perfect case; b, modeling the position of the solar system in the galaxy and the known universe, the distance ladder puts real numbers on that model.
astronomy/measuring-distance.757e1c02e33b: Two identical stars: one is three times farther away than the other. The farther one looks…
astronomy/measuring-distance.518b816e4ece: Nobody can stretch a tape measure to a star. So how do astronomers know that Proxima Centauri is four point two light-years away and the Andromeda Galaxy is two point five million light-years away? The answer is hiding in your thumb, in stars that pulse like a heartbeat, and in stretched-out light.
astronomy/measuring-distance.95d7f958a7f0: Rung two, Standard candles: know how bright it really is, and you know how far it is
astronomy/measuring-distance.f11ddd46490b: Hydrogen-alpha is at six hundred fifty-six point three nanometers in the lab, but seven hundred twenty-one point nine nanometers in a galaxy. What is its redshift z?
astronomy/measuring-distance.592064f363c1: Hubble’s law: speed equals H zero times distance, with H zero about seventy kilometers per second per megaparsec, one megaparsec equals three point two six million light-years. So d equals v divided by H zero.
astronomy/measuring-distance.ed84ea9a77c6: Proxima Centauri. The nearest star to the Sun. A small, cool red dwarf, far too faint to see without a telescope. It belongs to the Alpha Centauri system, which you can see from the Southern Hemisphere. It has at least one planet, Proxima b, inside its habitable zone. Even the closest star shifts less than one arcsecond: smaller than a coin seen from five kilometers away.
astronomy/measuring-distance.65eb718ef049: d equals one divided by p equals one divided by zero point five equals two parsecs; two times three point two six — about six point five light-years.
astronomy/measuring-distance.75965080bd63: Inverse-square law: three times three equals nine.
astronomy/measuring-distance.a27f250c1f3f: Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid, V one, in the Andromeda “nebula” and showed it lies far outside the Milky Way. Andromeda was a whole other galaxy! Leavitt had died in nineteen twenty-one and never saw this.
astronomy/measuring-distance.4fc121dd6a15: Memory hint: Even the closest star shifts less than one arcsecond: smaller than a coin seen from five kilometers away.

Parallax angle p is HALF of the total shift between January and July, one radius of Earth’s orbit as the baseline. With a one AU baseline: distance in parsecs equals one divided by p in arcseconds. Halve the angle, double the distance. Below about zero point zero zero one arcseconds even Gaia’s measurements get too uncertain for single stars. Parsec equals the distance where p equals one arcsecond, about three point two six light-years.

The star that gave Cepheids their name. Its distance is also known from parallax, Hubble and Gaia, which is how the chart gets calibrated.
astronomy/measuring-distance.118c1259cec3: On plates of the Magellanic Clouds she found one thousand seven hundred seventy-seven variable stars, and noticed that the brighter Cepheids had longer periods.
astronomy/measuring-distance.ffc8e6f05e10: Nineteen oh eight, one thousand seven hundred seventy-seven variable stars

astronomy/moon-phases.89b6e464141c: The whole sunlit half faces Earth, so we see a complete bright disk, about day fifteen.
astronomy/moon-phases.0d178861ee14: The Moon orbits Earth once every twenty-seven point three days, but a full cycle of phases takes twenty-nine point five days, because Earth moves along its own orbit meanwhile.
astronomy/moon-phases.dc37ef2b76ff: Supports GSE S six E two A: develop and use a model to demonstrate the phases of the Moon by showing the relative positions of the Sun, Earth, and Moon.
astronomy/moon-phases.d18f33f517fb: Because of this motion, the Moon rises about fifty minutes later each day.
astronomy/moon-phases.36e279ba348d: Try it: count the days from one full Moon to the next. About twenty-nine or thirty.
astronomy/moon-phases.b1ef08457fc3: The real thing. A waxing crescent: only a thin sliver of the sunlit half is turned toward Earth.
astronomy/moon-phases.f24fde3922db: First quarter. Right half lit, about day seven. The Moon has traveled a quarter of the way around Earth. From Earth we see half of the sunlit half: the right half of the disk. It rises around noon and is highest in the sky at sunset. “Quarter” is about the orbit, one quarter of the way around, not the shape.
astronomy/moon-phases.3bb7cab8f0fa: The real thing. “Earthrise”, taken from lunar orbit by Apollo eight astronaut Bill Anders on December twenty-fourth, nineteen sixty-eight. Seen from the Moon, Earth has phases too: only part of it is sunlit.
astronomy/moon-phases.479f1fe7642e: Common mix-up: The orbit is tilted about five degrees, so we don’t get eclipses every month.
astronomy/moon-phases.48e50bf6439d: The Moon. Reflects sunlight, orbits Earth. The Moon orbits Earth once every twenty-seven point three days, but a full cycle of phases takes twenty-nine point five days, because Earth moves along its own orbit meanwhile. The Moon spins once per orbit, so the same side always faces Earth. The far side is not always dark: it gets sunlight during the new Moon! Half lit, always. We just see different amounts of that half.
astronomy/moon-phases.8c7f6d2dc30b: Each day’s phase, calculated from the Moon’s real motion, accurate to about half a day. Click a day to see that night’s Moon and its position in the three D model above.
astronomy/moon-phases.6667a2db3b36: The Sun. Lights the Moon. The Moon makes no light of its own. Moonlight is sunlight bouncing off the Moon. The Sun always lights the half of the Moon that faces it. The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel. It is one hundred fifty million kilometers away. Moonlight is recycled sunlight.
astronomy/moon-phases.948c3888b636: The real thing. The far side of the Moon, mapped by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. We never see this side from Earth, because the Moon always keeps the same face toward us.
astronomy/moon-phases.6b6fd6250dff: The real thing. A full Moon, photographed through a telescope from Madison, Alabama on October twenty-second, twenty ten. The whole side facing us is lit. Three thousand four hundred seventy-four kilometers across, about three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away
astronomy/moon-phases.4efcfa516d3e: Target the misconception “phases are Earth’s shadow”: stop the slider at first quarter and ask where Earth’s shadow points, to the right, away from the Moon. Turn on “eight phases” and stress that every small Moon is half lit, with the lit side facing the Sun.
astronomy/moon-phases.3c8a12593b65: Memory hint: “Quarter” is about the orbit, one quarter of the way around, not the shape.
astronomy/moon-phases.5b9d8afacd5e: Its rotation and revolution take the same time, twenty-seven point three days. The far side gets sunlight too.
astronomy/moon-phases.c76cb848c4a7: From one new Moon to the next takes about twenty-nine point five days, roughly one month. The word “month” comes from “Moon”.
astronomy/moon-phases.de4a08473a71: A twenty-nine point five day cycle
astronomy/moon-phases.c2110b606f95: The Moon’s orbit is tilted about five degrees, so it usually passes above or below Earth’s shadow
astronomy/moon-phases.2b92eea08ac0: Left half lit, about day twenty-two
astronomy/moon-phases.073455cdc947: Earth’s shadow usually misses the Moon, because the Moon’s orbit is tilted about five degrees.
astronomy/moon-phases.d22c2b251e3b: Three thousand four hundred seventy-four kilometers, about zero point five degrees
astronomy/moon-phases.9cd5533e22f2: The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel. It is one hundred fifty million kilometers away.
astronomy/moon-phases.67b83e83226f: Full Moon. Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. The whole sunlit half faces Earth, so we see a complete bright disk, about day fifteen. It rises at sunset and sets at sunrise, so it shines all night. Earth’s shadow usually misses the Moon, because the Moon’s orbit is tilted about five degrees. Full Moon: Sun and Moon on opposite sides of the sky.
astronomy/moon-phases.c602558115b6: The Moon reflects only about twelve percent of the sunlight hitting it, like worn asphalt; it looks bright only because the night sky is so dark.
astronomy/moon-phases.c5442a1b66b9: Third quarter. Left half lit, about day twenty-two. The Moon has traveled three quarters of the way around Earth. We see the left half of the disk lit. It rises around midnight and is high in the sky at sunrise, so you can see it in the morning. Also called “last quarter”.
astronomy/moon-phases.37bee3a0457d: Moon’s orbit. One trip around Earth. The Moon is about three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away, roughly thirty Earth diameters. This model is not to scale. Seen from above the North Pole, the Moon moves counterclockwise, west to east. Because of this motion, the Moon rises about fifty minutes later each day. Counterclockwise from above, like Earth’s spin.
astronomy/moon-phases.1f5098e321e1: Waning crescent. A thin sliver, lit on the left. Only a thin sliver of the sunlit half still faces us. Look for it in the eastern sky just before sunrise. A few days later the cycle starts again with a new Moon, about twenty-nine point five days after the last one. Crescent equals a thin “C” or backwards “C” shape.
astronomy/moon-phases.2980970cd6d4: About twenty-seven percent of Earth’s width, narrower than the continental US, about four thousand five hundred kilometers coast to coast.
astronomy/moon-phases.1e3f6680c747: Common mix-up: It looks like a half Moon, but it is called a quarter because the Moon is one quarter of the way through its orbit.

astronomy/moon-phases.b82373afef75: Three hundred eighty-four thousand four hundred kilometers, about sixty Earth radii, about one point two eight light-seconds
astronomy/moon-phases.6cfbde01ad58: The Moon is about three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away, roughly thirty Earth diameters. This model is not to scale.
astronomy/moon-phases.26e64a62026c: The Moon doesn’t really change shape. As it orbits Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half. Drag the slider and compare the big three D view with the view from Earth.
astronomy/moon-phases.dbc2cb3e7392: The Moon moves about thirteen degrees east among the stars each day, about twelve degrees relative to the Sun, so Earth must spin a little longer to catch up with it.

astronomy/planets-moons.e07e65565897: GALILEAN MOONS. Four big moons. Galileo found them in January sixteen ten with a small telescope. Seeing moons circle another planet showed that not everything orbits Earth. Io, Europa and Ganymede tug on each other in a one to two to four rhythm, an orbital resonance. Those regular tugs keep their orbits slightly oval, so Jupiter’s tides flex them and heat their insides: volcanoes on Io, an ocean under Europa’s ice. You can see all four with ordinary binoculars as tiny dots next to Jupiter. MEMORY HINT. Order outward: “I Eat Green Cheese” equals Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto. Common mix-up: A resonance does not mean the moons line up all together: in fact Io, Europa and Ganymede can never all be on the same side of Jupiter at once.

astronomy/rocketry.73a407e62f72: The rocket equation. Delta v equals exhaust velocity times the natural log of the quantity m zero divided by m sub f. Written down by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in nineteen oh three. Delta v is the total change in speed a rocket can make. It depends only on exhaust speed and the mass ratio: full mass m zero divided by empty mass m sub f. Reaching low Earth orbit needs about nine point four kilometers per second of delta v, seven point eight kilometers per second of orbital speed plus about one point five kilometers per second lost to gravity and drag. With exhaust velocity equals three kilometers per second, getting nine point four kilometers per second from one stage would need m zero divided by m sub f about twenty-three: the rocket would have to be about ninety-six percent fuel. That is why real rockets use stages. More fuel helps less and less: the mass ratio sits inside a logarithm. Delta v is not the top speed you will see. Gravity and drag eat part of it on the way up.
astronomy/rocketry.8916954c6faa: Staging. Throw away what you no longer need. When a stage runs out of fuel, it drops off with its empty tanks and engines. The rest of the rocket no longer has to carry that dead weight. Saturn five had three stages; Falcon nine and Long March five have two, plus side boosters on Long March five. Engines on upper stages are designed for vacuum: hydrogen engines like the R L one zero reach exhaust speeds of about four point five kilometers per second. Falcon nine first stages now fly back and land so they can be reused; some boosters have flown more than twenty times. Staging equals a relay race: each runner hands on a lighter rocket. Stages are not dropped because they are “used up” like a battery. They are dropped because empty tanks are heavy and useless.

astronomy/rocketry.29d1461ceb2b: What “orbit” means. Fast enough sideways to keep missing Earth. Space officially starts at about one hundred kilometers, the Kármán line. Reaching it takes about one point four kilometers per second straight up, or just a few minutes of flight. A suborbital flight needs only a small fraction of the energy of an orbital flight. Think of a suborbital flight like a quick hop to one hundred kilometers and back. In orbit the engines switch off. Thrust, in newtons, equals mass thrown out per second, kilograms per second, times exhaust speed, meters per second. Double either one and the thrust doubles. Engineers like high exhaust speed best, because it gives more push from each kilogram of fuel. One F one engine of the Saturn five burned about two point six tonnes of propellant every second, with an exhaust speed of about two point six kilometers per second: about six point eight million newtons. astronomy/rocketry.6b2b5bf5cbd1: Action and reaction. Newton’s third law makes rockets go. When the rocket pushes gas backward, the gas pushes the rocket forward with a force of exactly the same size. A rocket does not push against the air or the ground. It works even better in the vacuum of space, where no air gets in the way of the exhaust. In nineteen twenty a New York Times editorial mocked Robert Goddard for claiming rockets could work in a vacuum. In nineteen sixty-nine, as Apollo eleven flew to the Moon, the paper printed a correction. A garden hose kicks back in your hands for the same reason: water pushed one way pushes you the other way. Push gas back, gas pushes you forward. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Rockets do not need air to push on. The flame is not pushing the ground; the rocket is pushing its own exhaust.

astronomy/seasons.9a03c33ef717: Flashlight sim: have students compare Atlanta’s spot size and day length in June versus December, and include BOTH in their explanation, more concentrated rays and longer days. Note: sizes and distances in the three D model are not to scale.
astronomy/seasons.e1d41e8a33fc: The equator divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. It is at zero degrees latitude.
astronomy/seasons.2685d23f8cbe: June solstice. About June twenty-first, longest day in the north. The north end of the axis leans toward the Sun. The noon Sun is directly over the Tropic of Cancer, twenty-three point five degrees north. Summer begins in the Northern Hemisphere; winter begins in the Southern Hemisphere. The Arctic has twenty-four-hour daylight. Solstice equals “Sun stands still”: the Sun reaches its highest noon point of the year in the north.
astronomy/seasons.bd7b1e3fafc7: September equinox. About September twenty-second, day equals night. Again, neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun. The noon Sun is directly over the equator. Autumn begins in the north, spring in the south. Two equinoxes a year: March and September.
astronomy/seasons.d6747269bfdd: Supports GSE S six E two c: analyze and interpret data to relate the tilt of the Earth to the distribution of sunlight throughout the year and its effect on seasons, also reviews rotation, day and night, and revolution, year.
astronomy/seasons.b5e55eb15cf0: Around January third Earth is closest to the Sun, perihelion, about one hundred forty-seven million kilometers; around July fourth it is farthest, aphelion, about one hundred fifty-two million kilometers. Yet January is winter in the north! Distance changes only about three percent, a tiny effect.
astronomy/seasons.4e0ac3aaed3a: About December twenty-first, shortest day in the north
astronomy/seasons.e87af2b959ab: Earth’s distance from the Sun changes by only about three percent: from one hundred forty-seven to one hundred fifty-two million kilometers.
astronomy/seasons.c0f82cc6c36a: The most common misconception is “summer happens when Earth is closer to the Sun.” Have students slide to about January third, perihelion, read the distance, and check the northern season; then press “What if no tilt?” to show that no tilt means no seasons.
astronomy/seasons.d372c7f2a9a5: Day-night line. Boundary between the lit half and the dark half. Sunlight always lights half of Earth. The edge between day and night is called the circle of illumination. As Earth rotates, places cross this line at sunrise and sunset. In June the whole Arctic stays inside the lit half all day: twenty-four hours of daylight, the “midnight Sun”. Antarctica has twenty-four hours of night. Half lit, always, just like the Moon.
astronomy/seasons.3a8d4a0ce3ed: Tropic of Cancer, twenty-three point five degrees north
astronomy/seasons.92d4669e8018: About March twentieth, day equals night
astronomy/seasons.7e58d2a0f445: Rotation: Earth spins west to east on its axis once every twenty-four hours. This causes day and night.
astronomy/seasons.424be25e3ea4: Earth spins west to east on its axis once every twenty-four hours. The half facing the Sun has day; the half facing away has night.
astronomy/seasons.c0884af05f55: Earth’s axis is tilted about twenty-three point five degrees from “straight up” compared with its orbit.
astronomy/seasons.6aeec3430da3: About three hundred sixty-five and a quarter days
astronomy/seasons.0feb93ea9e36: The axis tilts about twenty-three point five degrees and always points toward Polaris. So for half the year the north leans toward the Sun, and for the other half the south does.
astronomy/seasons.d6bf3a5345ed: On the June solstice the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, twenty-three point five degrees north.
astronomy/seasons.6f6962a9ee9a: Tilt of twenty-three point five degrees
astronomy/seasons.5183e2f68a61: Day and night are about twelve hours each everywhere

astronomy/seasons.1eaf7be861c7: Day and night are about twelve hours everywhere. Spring begins in the north, autumn in the south.
astronomy/seasons.a23016aacbcc: The real thing. The midnight Sun at Nordkapp, Norway. Far north in summer, the North Pole is tilted toward the Sun so much that the Sun never sets. About seventy-one degrees north. Georgia is about thirty-three degrees north.
astronomy/seasons.fd2ca19183a4: The real thing. Earth seen by a weather satellite at the solstices and equinoxes, December twenty ten to September twenty eleven. Look at how the line between day and night changes its tilt.
astronomy/seasons.b2b366938397: Tropic of Capricorn, twenty-three point five degrees south
astronomy/seasons.e789b0954491: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
astronomy/seasons.98f1378119ef: March equinox. About March twentieth, day equals night. Neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun. The noon Sun is directly over the equator. Day and night are about twelve hours everywhere. Spring begins in the north, autumn in the south. “Equinox” means “equal night”.
astronomy/seasons.9188682963c3: Earth is closest, perihelion, around January third, during northern winter, and farthest, aphelion, around July fourth, during northern summer.
astronomy/seasons.e3d0a191a046: Common mix-up: “The Sun is straight overhead at noon” is only true between the Tropics, and only on one or two days a year. In Atlanta the noon Sun is always toward the south and never higher than about eighty degrees.
astronomy/seasons.d73ebd3bb85d: Equator and tropics. Where the Sun can be directly overhead. The equator divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. It is at zero degrees latitude. On the June solstice the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, twenty-three point five degrees north. On the December solstice it is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, twenty-three point five degrees south. Outside the tropics the Sun is never straight overhead. The tropics are twenty-three point five degrees from the equator, the same number as the tilt!
astronomy/seasons.2361bd0de90e: Revolution: Earth travels around the Sun once every three hundred sixty-five and a quarter days. That is one year.
astronomy/seasons.8e8eaea19114: The noon Sun is directly over the Tropic of Cancer, twenty-three point five degrees north.
astronomy/seasons.60d40d798aa4: The real Sun is one hundred nine times wider than Earth and about one hundred fifty million kilometers away. This model is not to scale.
astronomy/seasons.148bbafe6689: One revolution is one year. The extra quarter day becomes a leap day every four years.
astronomy/seasons.f314d2370011: Tilted axis, twenty-three point five degrees
astronomy/seasons.ead5455c06a5: On the December solstice it is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, twenty-three point five degrees south. Outside the tropics the Sun is never straight overhead.
astronomy/seasons.7ac612ba4838: In June the whole Arctic stays inside the lit half all day: twenty-four hours of daylight, the “midnight Sun”. Antarctica has twenty-four hours of night.
astronomy/seasons.fe96a4c65f4c: Memory hint: The tropics are twenty-three point five degrees from the equator, the same number as the tilt!
astronomy/seasons.eb7ac853e1bb: Perihelion is around January third, which is winter in the north. That proves distance does not cause seasons.
astronomy/seasons.94745a96e6c3: December solstice. About December twenty-first, shortest day in the north. The north end of the axis leans away from the Sun, it still points at Polaris! The noon Sun is directly over the Tropic of Capricorn, twenty-three point five degrees south. Winter begins in the north; summer begins in the south, so people in Australia often spend Christmas at the beach. Two weeks later, Earth is at its closest point to the Sun, in winter!
astronomy/seasons.9dbb667a7037: Summer begins in the Northern Hemisphere; winter begins in the Southern Hemisphere. The Arctic has twenty-four-hour daylight.
astronomy/seasons.5dd312c53e0c: The real thing. The “Blue Marble”, taken on December seventh, nineteen seventy-two, two weeks before the December solstice. The South Pole is tilted toward the Sun, so Antarctica, bottom, is in full sunlight.
astronomy/seasons.608221d89e60: Earth. Spins once a day, orbits once a year. Rotation: Earth spins west to east on its axis once every twenty-four hours. This causes day and night. Revolution: Earth travels around the Sun once every three hundred sixty-five and a quarter days. That is one year. Because Earth spins toward the east, the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west. ROtation equals ROlling in place, spin. REVolution equals going aRound the Sun.
astronomy/seasons.85a61aaa0488: The North Pole has twenty-four hours of daylight
astronomy/seasons.256349220e0e: Memory hint: Tilt plus orbit equals seasons. Press “What if no tilt?” to test it.
astronomy/seasons.ddb15ebc7d6e: The Sun does NOT always rise due east and set due west. Pick a place and a date to see the Sun’s whole arc across the sky, and how the shadow of a one-meter stick swings around. Summer arcs are high and long; winter arcs are low and short.
astronomy/seasons.3e09f64301ae: Earth orbits the Sun once every three hundred sixty-five and a quarter days. The extra quarter day adds up to a leap day, February twenty-ninth, every four years.
astronomy/seasons.07535e3360a8: About September twenty-second, day equals night
astronomy/seasons.d837afdc5b57: The Sun. Source of light and heat. The Sun always lights exactly half of Earth. That half has daytime. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. The real Sun is one hundred nine times wider than Earth and about one hundred fifty million kilometers away. This model is not to scale. The Sun stays put. Earth’s tilt and orbit make the seasons.
astronomy/seasons.b7a01157d8be: Big idea: Seasons happen because Earth’s axis is tilted twenty-three point five degrees. The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets more direct sunlight and longer days.
astronomy/seasons.c1c8ed8a40c1: Tilted axis, twenty-three point five degrees. The real cause of the seasons. Earth’s axis is tilted about twenty-three point five degrees from “straight up” compared with its orbit. The axis always points the same way in space, toward Polaris, the North Star, all year long. So in June the north end leans toward the Sun, and in December it leans away. Tilt and orbit equals seasons. Press “What if no tilt?” to test it.
astronomy/seasons.603110976d84: About June twenty-first, longest day in the north
astronomy/seasons.6eb25949b273: Earth’s orbit. Almost a perfect circle. Earth’s distance from the Sun changes by only about three percent: from one hundred forty-seven to one hundred fifty-two million kilometers. Earth is closest, perihelion, around January third, during northern winter, and farthest, aphelion, around July fourth, during northern summer. If distance caused seasons, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time. They don’t. Closest in January, yet it’s cold in Georgia: distance is NOT the reason.
astronomy/seasons.e3b0614a71df: One rotation takes about twenty-four hours. The half of Earth facing the Sun has day.

astronomy/sky-tonight.53d7d8b91453: Atlanta, Georgia, November twenty-first, twenty twenty-six at one thirty a.m.: full night, Sun negative seventy degrees. The Moon is ninety-two percent lit and forty degrees up in the west. Planets up: Mars, east, nineteen degrees; Jupiter, east, twenty-one degrees; Saturn, west, twenty degrees. About five thousand real stars are on this map: every star down to magnitude six, roughly what your eyes can see from a dark countryside. The whole sky turns fifteen degrees every hour because Earth spins from west to east. The sky turns once in twenty-three hours, fifty-six minutes. Planets always stay near the yellow dashed line, the ecliptic. It is the flat plane of the solar system seen edge-on. Each day the Moon moves about thirteen degrees east against the stars, so it rises about fifty minutes later each night. Stars twinkle; planets mostly shine steadily. If a bright "star" sits on the ecliptic and isn't on a star chart, it's a planet. Polaris is NOT the brightest star in the sky. It is about forty-eighth. It is famous because it barely moves: it sits almost exactly above Earth's North Pole.

astronomy/small-bodies.c4f223d04b54: Halley’s Comet. Edmond Halley predicted its return for seventeen fifty-eight using Newton’s laws, the first comet known to come back. In nineteen eighty-six the European spacecraft Giotto flew within six hundred kilometers of its nucleus: a dark, potato-shaped lump about fifteen kilometers long. Its orbit is tilted and goes around backward compared with the planets. Dust it left behind causes two meteor showers: the Eta Aquariids, May, and the Orionids, October. Comets live on long, stretched ellipses: fast near the Sun, slow far away.

astronomy/small-bodies.490fa645e187: Asteroid Apophis will pass Earth on April thirteenth, twenty twenty-nine, closer than some satellites, and will be visible without a telescope. It is about three hundred forty meters. It will not hit us.

astronomy/small-bodies.263c444eaef8: Besides eight planets, the Sun is circled by millions of asteroids, comets and dwarf planets. Where they live tells us what they are made of.
astronomy/small-bodies.d93f2ce6dbe3: Simplified physics: each impactor is six hundred kilograms at six kilometers per second with momentum boost beta equals three — DART measured about three point six; asteroid density two thousand kilograms per cubic meter. Pushing along the direction of motion changes the orbital period, so the shift keeps growing, about three times delta v times t; sideways or sunward pushes do not keep adding up.

astronomy/small-bodies.cd514df32309: Pluto’s stretched orbit sometimes brings it closer to the Sun than Neptune, last time nineteen seventy-nine to nineteen ninety-nine, but the two can never collide: Pluto goes around twice for every three Neptune orbits.

astronomy/small-bodies.d2e8c44ca274: Oort Cloud, schematic. A giant, roughly spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the whole solar system. We infer it from the orbits of comets that fall in from every direction. A passing star or the pull of the Milky Way can nudge an Oort Cloud object inward, and it becomes a long-period comet like Hale-Bopp. Its outer edge may reach a third of the way to the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, two hundred sixty-eight thousand astronomical units. Short trips, less than two hundred years, Kuiper Belt comets; very long trips, Oort Cloud comets.

astronomy/star-life.cef7be7bd818: Hydrogen. Big Bang. Made in the first few minutes after the Big Bang, thirteen point eight billion years ago. Water and every organic molecule, about sixty-two percent of your atoms!

astronomy/star-life.1d78bf1f38e6: This lesson goes well beyond grade six, toward high-school Earth and Space Science or Astronomy: reading the H R diagram, the mass-luminosity-lifetime relation, the Stefan-Boltzmann law, L is proportional to R squared times T to the fourth, Wien’s displacement law and nucleosynthesis. It connects to “the Sun is a star” in S six E one and to the periodic table in physical science.

astronomy/sun-stars.252f1b561ac5: Data: SILSO, Royal Observatory of Belgium, smoothed sunspot numbers, approximate values; the dashed line after twenty twenty-five is a rough forecast. The number of spots drawn on the disc is only roughly proportional to the sunspot number.
astronomy/sun-stars.5ee036a87b0d: The tops of the convection cells show on the surface as granules, each roughly one thousand kilometers across.
astronomy/sun-stars.0fbe28a2be74: Radiative zone. Energy travels as light. Energy moves outward as light, photons, that is absorbed and given off again and again. Because of this zig-zag path, energy can take tens of thousands of years or more to cross this zone. The temperature drops from about seven million degrees Celsius to about two million degrees Celsius. It runs from about one quarter to seven tenths of the way to the surface. Radiative equals radiation: light bouncing like a pinball.
astronomy/sun-stars.6f0149fe37a4: It is over one million degrees Celsius, far hotter than the surface below it.
astronomy/sun-stars.ec6ba9bc82d1: Supports GSE S six E one, the solar system and the universe, including S six E one B, the Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way; modeling our place in the universe. Suggested flow: run the “Energy journey” story to trace fusion, radiative zone, convection zone, photosphere, Earth, then use the Solar activity slider to discuss the eleven-year sunspot cycle and space weather.
astronomy/sun-stars.22313f91de6d: Convection zone. Hot gas rises, cool gas sinks. Hot gas rises, cools near the top and sinks again, like a pot of boiling soup, convection currents. These currents carry the energy up to the surface. The tops of the convection cells show on the surface as granules, each roughly one thousand kilometers across. It is the outer thirty percent of the Sun: about two million degrees Celsius at the bottom and five thousand five hundred degrees Celsius at the top. Convection equals hot rises, cool sinks, like a lava lamp.
astronomy/sun-stars.ea9ed1045fc5: Sunspots. Cooler, darker patches. Darker, cooler areas on the photosphere, about three thousand five hundred to four thousand five hundred degrees Celsius. They form where strong magnetic fields block hot gas from rising. Their number rises and falls in an eleven-year cycle, solar minimum, solar maximum. Try the activity slider! Many sunspots are larger than the whole Earth. A sunspot is cooler, not cold. It only looks dark next to even brighter gas.
astronomy/sun-stars.74c06fd34625: The Sun fuses about six hundred million tonnes of hydrogen every second.
astronomy/sun-stars.d157892d1260: Protostar. A baby star heating up. A collapsing clump heats up as gravity squeezes it tighter. It glows from heat, but fusion has not started yet. When its core reaches about ten million degrees Celsius, hydrogen fusion begins and a true star is born. Proto equals first: a protostar is a star before fusion.
astronomy/sun-stars.7fd0563a9636: Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen: the longest stage. The star fuses hydrogen into helium in its core. Gravity pulling in is balanced by pressure pushing out, so the star stays steady. About ninety percent of stars, including the Sun, are main-sequence stars. More massive stars are hotter, bluer and brighter, and they use up their fuel much faster. Big stars live fast and die young.
astronomy/sun-stars.cc309ad7b35b: Core. The fusion power plant. The hottest part of the Sun: about fifteen million degrees Celsius. Hydrogen nuclei crash together and fuse into helium, nuclear fusion, releasing enormous energy. The Sun fuses about six hundred million tonnes of hydrogen every second. It reaches out to about one quarter of the Sun’s radius. Core equals fusion: hydrogen and hydrogen react to form helium and energy.
astronomy/sun-stars.f80af374cfe8: Chromosphere. A thin reddish layer. A thin layer of the Sun’s atmosphere just above the photosphere; “chromo” means color. Normally too faint to see next to the bright photosphere; it appears as a pinkish-red rim during a total solar eclipse. Strangely, it gets hotter with height, up to about twenty thousand degrees Celsius. Chromo equals color: the pink-red layer.
astronomy/sun-stars.615d202a9143: Sunspots are cooler, darker patches where tangled magnetic fields poke through the Sun’s surface. Their number rises and falls about every eleven years. Drag the year slider to watch the Sun change from nineteen fifty to twenty thirty, or press.
astronomy/sun-stars.cfdb87257c53: Time to reach Earth, one hundred fifty million kilometers
astronomy/sun-stars.e39941174b3d: Corona. The Sun’s outer atmosphere. The outermost layer, stretching millions of kilometers into space. It is over one million degrees Celsius, far hotter than the surface below it. During a total solar eclipse it appears as a pearly white crown. It streams outward as the solar wind; when the solar wind hits Earth’s magnetic field it can cause auroras. Corona equals crown, it looks like one during an eclipse.
astronomy/sun-stars.497632c582cc: The real thing. The same Sun in ultraviolet light, seen by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. The colors are false; this light shows the hot gas just above the surface.
astronomy/sun-stars.e3ac167f1b79: With more spots come more solar flares and coronal mass ejections, CMEs, so Earth gets more auroras, and stronger ones, and satellites, radio and power grids are more likely to be disturbed. Cycle twenty-five peaked around twenty twenty-four; in May of that year a huge geomagnetic storm brought auroras as far south as Florida.
astronomy/sun-stars.ab075e7213b9: In the core, hydrogen nuclei join to make helium and release huge energy. The Sun fuses about six hundred million tonnes of hydrogen every second.
astronomy/sun-stars.833a029442aa: The real thing. The Sun in X-rays, from the Yohkoh satellite. The bright loops are gas in the corona that is millions of degrees hot.
astronomy/sun-stars.d3538c4037d0: Very fast CME, Carrington event, eighteen fifty-nine
astronomy/sun-stars.50016038e325: Average length of Cycles nineteen to twenty-four: about ten point nine years, shortest about nine point seven, longest about twelve point five, hence the “eleven-year cycle”. Peaks vary a lot: Cycle nineteen was about two point five times as strong as Cycle twenty-four.
astronomy/sun-stars.618d359f2749: Common mix-up: An aurora is not reflected sunlight, and the solar wind does not light the sky directly. Fast particles hit oxygen and nitrogen about one hundred to three hundred kilometers up and make them glow: oxygen gives green and red, nitrogen blue-purple.
astronomy/sun-stars.1368d168f012: Strong magnetic fields block hot gas from rising, so sunspots are about one thousand five hundred degrees Celsius cooler.
astronomy/sun-stars.7f8adde89cfa: Strangely, it gets hotter with height, up to about twenty thousand degrees Celsius.
astronomy/sun-stars.a907e703fb65: This star's main-sequence life: about ten billion years
astronomy/sun-stars.00a042ec9038: The Sun is four point six billion years old, about halfway through its life. In about five billion years it will become a red giant and finally a white dwarf.
astronomy/sun-stars.b80b3a35b2e1: Stars spend about ninety percent of their lives fusing hydrogen on the main sequence.
astronomy/sun-stars.ac056f79ce84: They are not really cold: a sunspot is about three thousand five hundred to four thousand five hundred degrees Celsius, just cooler than the five thousand five hundred degrees Celsius surface around it. Strong magnetic fields block hot gas from rising there, so the spot looks darker. On its own in the night sky, a sunspot would shine brighter than the full Moon.
astronomy/sun-stars.7b8b7f0339f3: The Sun is about one point three nine million kilometers across, yet it is only medium-sized; some stars are one thousand times wider.
astronomy/sun-stars.01e61d2d8895: Common mix-up: The energy is ancient by the time it escapes, but the final trip from the surface to Earth takes only about eight minutes.
astronomy/sun-stars.1edba3a31b5a: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, H R, sorts stars by surface temperature and brightness. Surface temperature goes across, hottest on the LEFT. Brightness goes up, with the Sun equal to one. Most stars fall on the main-sequence band from top-left to bottom-right. Click anywhere to read the chart, or play “Place the star”.
astronomy/sun-stars.58eccf3aa3b9: A star twenty-five times the Sun’s mass explodes. What could be left?
astronomy/sun-stars.21f55c17735a: In “Life of a star”, have students compare a one-solar-mass and a twenty-five-solar-mass star to conclude that mass determines a star’s fate. The H R game works as an exit ticket: students mark the Sun and explain its position.
astronomy/sun-stars.f8b575ea8f14: When its core reaches about ten million degrees Celsius, hydrogen fusion begins and a true star is born.
astronomy/sun-stars.2c4e23d679d3: Red giant. Swollen, cooler outer layers. When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the core shrinks and heats up while the outer layers swell and cool. The star becomes hundreds of times wider and glows red. In about five billion years the Sun will become a red giant and may swallow Mercury and Venus. Red giant equals huge but cooler on the outside.
astronomy/sun-stars.00d19601a8ec: The temperature drops from about seven million degrees Celsius to about two million degrees Celsius.
astronomy/sun-stars.54823da465ec: The real thing. The Sun in ordinary light, or white light, photographed through a small telescope with a full solar filter. The dark dots are sunspots on the photosphere. One million three hundred ninety-two thousand seven hundred kilometers across.
astronomy/sun-stars.666b1d711851: Memory hint: The “butterfly pattern”: each new cycle’s spots appear about thirty degrees from the equator, then show up closer and closer to it. Watch the spot belts on the disc move!
astronomy/sun-stars.b99cf021d046: It is the outer thirty percent of the Sun: about two million degrees Celsius at the bottom and five thousand five hundred degrees Celsius at the top.
astronomy/sun-stars.c89fe2f8acdb: Note: interior layer thicknesses use real proportions, core about inner one quarter of the radius, convection zone about outer thirty percent; the chromosphere and corona are exaggerated so they can be seen. Lifetimes are approximate.
astronomy/sun-stars.b8a42577b009: The Sun’s eleven-year heartbeat: the sunspot cycle
astronomy/sun-stars.8f54d78b073b: About ninety percent of stars, including the Sun, are main-sequence stars.
astronomy/sun-stars.86a05daef2e0: Blue stars can be over thirty thousand degrees Celsius; red stars are about three thousand degrees Celsius.
astronomy/sun-stars.9c81dbe0dfc3: In about five billion years the Sun will become a red giant and may swallow Mercury and Venus.
astronomy/sun-stars.4d5c51c43427: The hottest part of the Sun: about fifteen million degrees Celsius.
astronomy/sun-stars.aa6288cea903: Near Earth the solar wind is extremely thin: only about five particles in every cubic centimetre. Air has about twenty-five billion billion.
astronomy/sun-stars.7b69b4ced454: reached Earth in about seventeen point six hours
astronomy/sun-stars.b31d63907844: Photosphere. The visible “surface”. The layer we see: light escapes into space from here. About five thousand five hundred degrees Celsius. It is not solid. You could not stand on it; it is glowing gas a few hundred kilometers thick. It is covered with bubbling granules and, at times, dark sunspots. Photo equals light: the photosphere is the “light sphere”.
astronomy/sun-stars.2dc9ae2e002f: The real thing. The “Pillars of Creation” in the Eagle Nebula, photographed by Hubble. New stars are being born inside these huge clouds of gas and dust. About seven thousand light-years away.
astronomy/sun-stars.d55a4e0de0da: The Sun is about one hundred fifty million kilometers away, so sunlight takes eight minutes twenty seconds to arrive. You see the Sun as it was eight minutes ago.

astronomy/telescopes-light.f2b601041bac: Radio waves. longer than thirty centimeters. Radio waves pass through clouds and even work in daytime, so radio telescopes can observe in any weather. Radio waves are so long that a dish must be enormous to see sharp detail. China’s FAST is five hundred meters across, or one thousand six hundred forty feet. That’s the size of thirty soccer fields. Several dishes far apart can be linked to act like one giant telescope. In twenty nineteen, eight observatories linked across the whole Earth took the first picture of a black hole. Radio equals longest waves, lowest energy, biggest dishes.
astronomy/telescopes-light.9bb236c33fea: Gamma rays. shorter than zero point zero one nanometers. The most energetic light there is: one gamma-ray photon can carry millions of times the energy of a visible-light photon. Earth’s atmosphere absorbs them completely, which protects life on the ground. Space telescopes like NASA’s Fermi catch them directly. Ground telescopes can only see the faint blue flash a very high-energy gamma ray makes when it smashes into the upper air. Gamma equals the most energetic. Shortest wave, highest energy.
astronomy/telescopes-light.8a65d5b51687: X-rays. zero point zero one to ten nanometers. X-ray telescopes show the hottest places in the universe, from millions to hundreds of millions of degrees. X-rays would go straight into a normal mirror, so telescopes like Chandra use nested, barrel-shaped mirrors that X-rays skim off at a very low angle, like a stone skipping on water. Our atmosphere stops all of them, so X-ray astronomy only became possible with rockets and satellites. X-rays, extreme heat, millions of degrees.
astronomy/telescopes-light.4666198141cb: Infrared. seven hundred nanometers to one millimeter. Infrared, IR, passes through dust that blocks visible light, so it shows baby stars hidden inside dark clouds. Light from the most distant galaxies has been stretched by the expanding universe from visible into infrared. That is why JWST is an infrared telescope. Water vapour in our air absorbs most infrared. Only a few “windows” get through, best from high, dry mountains. JWST has to be kept colder than minus two hundred thirty degrees Celsius so its own warmth doesn’t drown out the faint signals. Infrared equals “below red”: you feel it as warmth from a campfire.
astronomy/telescopes-light.523ff1c6ad6b: Visible light. four hundred to seven hundred nanometers. The only light your eyes can detect: violet through blue, green, yellow and orange to red. Violet is about four hundred nanometers, and red is about seven hundred nanometers. It is a tiny sliver of the whole spectrum, much less than one millionth of the range on this slider, but it is where the Sun gives off the most light. It passes through clear air, which is why telescopes have been built on the ground for four hundred years. Roy G Biv: red has the longest visible wave, violet the shortest.
astronomy/telescopes-light.eaf4f9cde91a: Ultraviolet. ten to four hundred nanometers. Ultraviolet, UV, light comes from things hotter than the Sun’s surface, such as young blue stars. The ozone layer absorbs almost all UV shorter than about three hundred nanometers. A little of the longer UV gets through: that is what gives you a sunburn. Hubble can see in ultraviolet because it orbits above the atmosphere. UV equals “beyond violet”: just past the violet end of the rainbow.
astronomy/telescopes-light.3dacea045dfc: Microwaves. one millimeter to thirty centimeters. Every direction in the sky glows faintly in microwaves: it is the cosmic microwave background, light left over from about three hundred eighty thousand years after the Big Bang. ALMA, sixty-six dishes on a five thousand meter high plateau in Chile, uses millimeter waves to see planets forming around young stars. The plateau is sixteen thousand four hundred feet high. Microwaves are often counted as short radio waves. Your microwave oven uses twelve centimeter waves; your Wi-Fi uses six or twelve centimeters. Microwaves: from the Big Bang’s afterglow to your kitchen.

Fresh air in the alveolus has MORE oxygen than the blood arriving from the body, so oxygen diffuses into the blood. Red blood cells carry it, and the heart pumps it to every cell. Bind: LDL particles stick to their matching receptors, like a key in a lock. Two. Coated pit: When enough receptors are full, a protein coat, clathrin, gray spikes, bends the membrane inward into a pit. Three. Pinch off: The pit pinches off into a coated vesicle carrying only LDL. Ribosome builds it: A ribosome on the rough ER builds the protein, following the DNA recipe from the nucleus. Two. Inside the ER: The new protein slides into the endoplasmic reticulum, ER, and travels through its tubes. Three. Vesicle: ER, Golgi: A vesicle buds off the ER and carries the protein to the Golgi body. Four. Golgi packs and labels: The Golgi body finishes the protein, packs it and labels where it must go. Five. biology/heredity.2ed91758a0aa: Punnett square. A grid that predicts offspring. One parent’s alleles go across the top, the other parent’s down the side. Each box is one possible offspring genotype. In a two times two square each box is a twenty-five percent chance. Named after the British geneticist Reginald Punnett, early nineteen hundreds. Letter on top and letter on the side react to form box.
biology/heredity.f5be2d97e94b: Dominant allele. Shows up even with only one copy. Written with a CAPITAL letter, like T. Capital T capital T and capital T lowercase t plants look the same: both are tall. Gregor Mendel found that one “factor” could hide another in his pea experiments, eighteen fifty-six to eighteen sixty-three. CAPITAL letter equals the “loud” allele that covers up the quiet one.
biology/heredity.95cb93d69b7a: Memory hint: one allele from parent one plus one allele from parent two equals two alleles.

biology/protein-synthesis.61af73855951: Ribosome. The protein factory. A ribosome has a small and a large subunit that clamp around the mRNA. It slides along the mRNA one codon at a time, or three bases at a time. It links amino acids together with peptide bonds.
biology/protein-synthesis.5238060df20a: Transfer RNA, tRNA. The delivery truck. Each tRNA carries one specific amino acid. Its anticodon pairs with a matching codon on the mRNA, like a key in a lock. biology/protein-synthesis.9e7b279d8b40: Its anticodon pairs with a matching codon on the mRNA, like a key in a lock. The anticodon has three bases.

biology/tonicity-labs.192434a3e71b: Eggs float in corn syrup and lose thirty to fifty percent of their mass in two to three days; the syrup is denser. Rinse and blot eggs before weighing, since syrup is sticky. Use the same scale, and tare it first. Common misconceptions: salt or sugar goes into the cell and “pulls” water; “a hypertonic solution has more water”; drawing a conclusion from one day or one egg.
biology/tonicity-labs.bae268ed93a9: Claim: The naked egg in corn syrup lost mass. Evidence: Its mass went from seventy point zero grams on Day two to thirty-eight point five grams on Day five, a change of minus forty-five point zero percent. In comparison, the simulated trials in distilled water changed by plus sixteen point six percent on average. Reasoning: The egg’s membrane is selectively permeable, so water can cross it but the sugar or salt mostly cannot. Corn syrup is hypertonic to the egg: it has more solute and less water than the inside of the egg. By osmosis, water moved from the high water concentration inside the egg to the low water concentration outside, so the egg lost mass.
biology/tonicity-labs.bcd36831b2e9: Lab tips: real classes use five to ten percent salt water and see plasmolysis within minutes; cells left in strong salt too long die and won’t recover. This reaction releases lots of energy. It powers some rockets and fuel-cell cars. Atoms are like LEGO bricks: take the model apart and build something new. Same bricks, new shape.

chemistry/states-of-matter.7651119ecf3b: Temperature. How fast the particles move on average. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles. Kinetic energy is motion energy. Hotter equals particles move faster. Colder equals particles move slower. At absolute zero, minus two hundred seventy-three degrees Celsius, particle motion is at its lowest possible level.

china/beijing-capital.fc342b33f7a3: Wanning Bridge. The oldest bridge on the axis, twelve eighty-five. First built in twelve eighty-five in the Yuan dynasty, and still used by traffic today. In Yuan times, grain boats on the Grand Canal passed under it into Jishuitan lake, today’s Shichahai, the canal’s northern end. Stone water creatures carved on its banks once watched the water level.
china/beijing-capital.a6a7dc544638: Nineteen eighty-seven was the year the Forbidden City was listed.
china/beijing-capital.dd8afaf75939: Tian’anmen. Gate of Heavenly Peace. Built in fourteen seventeen as the front gate of the Imperial City, and given the name Tian’anmen in sixteen fifty-one. On October first, nineteen forty-nine, the founding ceremony of the People’s Republic of China was held here. It appears on China’s national emblem.
china/beijing-capital.026bbf30a7e2: Approximate long-term monthly averages, rounded. Beijing: China Meteorological Administration climate data; Washington, D.C.: NOAA nineteen ninety-one to twenty twenty climate normals, Reagan National Airport.

More stops mean more points, but a stop only counts if you finish it before five p.m.! Lunch is added automatically and takes forty-five minutes.

china/beijing-capital.47833fab5a6c: Axis order south north: Yongdingmen; Temple of Heaven and Xiannongtan on either side; Zhengyangmen, the Square, Tian’anmen, the Forbidden City; Jingshan, Wanning Bridge, Drum and Bell: seven point eight kilometers on one line.
china/beijing-capital.4d8da9797097: The axis shows the ideal order of a Chinese capital: the most important buildings sit on the line, and everything else is arranged symmetrically on both sides. An ancient book, the Kaogongji, 考工记, says: “ancestral temple on the left, altar on the right; court in front, market behind.”
china/beijing-capital.e4dafbf1ddee: Beijing and Washington, D.C., are almost the same distance from the equator, yet their climates differ. Their latitudes are thirty-nine point nine degrees north and thirty-eight point nine degrees north, respectively. Hover over the charts to see each month.
china/beijing-capital.c28493b2176f: The Forbidden City, Palace Museum. Home of twenty-four Ming and Qing emperors. Built fourteen oh six to fourteen twenty. About nine hundred sixty-one meters long and seven hundred fifty-three meters wide, about seventy-two hectares, about one hundred thirty-five football fields, ringed by a ten-meter wall and a wide moat. About eight thousand seven hundred rooms, counted in 间, the space between four pillars. The Hall of Supreme Harmony on the axis is China’s largest surviving wooden hall. You go in through the Meridian Gate, 午门, in the south and out through the Gate of Divine Prowess, 神武门, in the north. It became the Palace Museum in nineteen twenty-five and a World Heritage Site in nineteen eighty-seven.
china/beijing-capital.097cb645600e: Zhengyangmen, Qianmen. Main south gate of the inner city. Built in fourteen nineteen. Its gate tower is about forty-three meters tall, or one hundred forty-one feet, the tallest of old Beijing’s city gates. In front stands an arrow tower with rows of small windows, built for archers to defend the gate. Outside it, Qianmen Street has been a busy shopping street for centuries.
china/beijing-capital.9eb1fa8f6ad9: Why would a city of more than twenty million people be built around one perfectly straight line? This line is seven point eight kilometers long, runs right through the emperor’s throne, and has been Beijing’s backbone for more than seven hundred years. That length is about four point eight miles. In twenty twenty-four it became a World Heritage Site.
china/beijing-capital.ca295a6fef4c: A siheyuan, 四合院, is a traditional Beijing home: four buildings around a courtyard. The lanes between rows of them are hutongs, 胡同. Change the season, the time of day and the way the house faces, and watch how sunlight reaches the main hall. Your question: why did old Beijing put the main hall facing south?
china/beijing-capital.320c18ab04e4: Temple of Heaven. Where emperors prayed for good harvests. Built in fourteen twenty for the Ming and Qing emperors to worship heaven and pray for good harvests. World Heritage Site since nineteen ninety-eight. The round Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests has three blue roofs: blue for the sky. It is about thirty-eight meters tall, or one hundred twenty-five feet. The park wall is round in the north and square in the south: “round heaven, square earth”, 天圆地方.
china/beijing-capital.16b9e5b73f32: In July twenty twenty-four, “Beijing Central Axis: A Building Ensemble Exhibiting the Ideal Order of the Chinese Capital” joined the World Heritage List as China’s fifty-ninth World Heritage Site. It has fifteen parts, including the Bell and Drum Towers, Wanning Bridge, Jingshan, the Forbidden City, Tian’anmen, the buildings of Tian’anmen Square, Zhengyangmen, the Temple of Heaven, the Xiannongtan altar and Yongdingmen.
china/beijing-capital.146b93d1d0d6: Jingshan. A man-made hill with the best view. Piled up in the Ming dynasty, largely from the earth dug out for the palace moat. About forty-five meters high, or one hundred fifty feet. The Wanchun Pavilion on top sits exactly on the axis. From the top you can see the golden roofs of the Forbidden City to the south and the Drum Tower to the north.
china/beijing-capital.ce00426dbb32: Today the line extends north to the Olympic Green, where the two thousand eight “Bird’s Nest” stadium and “Water Cube” stand on either side of it, and south toward Beijing Daxing International Airport, opened in twenty nineteen.
china/beijing-capital.d551a8e02b92: Xiannongtan, Altar of Agriculture. West of the axis. Built in fourteen twenty. Each spring the emperor came here to plough a small field himself, to show how important farming was. It sits to the west of the axis, balancing the Temple of Heaven to the east. Today it houses the Beijing Ancient Architecture Museum.

china/beijing-capital.77172be2216e: Bell Tower. The northern end of the axis. Rebuilt in seventeen forty-five to seventeen forty-seven during the Qing dynasty, entirely of brick and stone, so it could not burn down again. About forty-eight meters tall, or one hundred fifty-seven feet. Its bronze bell, cast in the Ming Yongle years, weighs about sixty-three tonnes: as much as five school buses. You have walked about seven point eight kilometers, about four point eight miles!
china/beijing-capital.dea48e02542c: Tian’anmen Square. One of the largest city squares in the world. About forty-four hectares: roughly eighty US football fields. A national flag-raising ceremony is held here at sunrise every day. On the axis: the Monument to the People’s Heroes, completed nineteen fifty-eight. On the sides: the Great Hall of the People, west, where the National People’s Congress meets, and the National Museum of China, east.

china/beijing-capital.724f309b342b: The Beijing Central Axis, 北京中轴线, runs from Yongdingmen Gate in the south to the Drum and Bell Towers in the north: about seven point eight kilometers. Drag the slider below, or press, to walk north. Each time you pass a landmark, its card pops up on the right.
china/beijing-capital.76e228fe5ae7: The National Mall runs west from the Capitol past the Washington Monument to the Lincoln Memorial: about three point two kilometers, two miles, also a planned city axis. Beijing’s Central Axis is about two point four times as long, and more than five hundred years older.
china/beijing-capital.009266573f22: Yongdingmen Gate. The southern start of the axis. Built in fifteen fifty-three, Ming dynasty, as the main south gate of the new outer city. The name means “Gate of Lasting Peace”. Torn down in nineteen fifty-seven to make room for traffic, then rebuilt in two thousand four from old drawings and photos. From here the axis runs dead straight north for about seven point eight kilometers, four point eight miles.
china/beijing-capital.c8b949c2fa30: Note: the three D model is schematic. Buildings are enlarged, and positions and distances are approximate.

china/china-space.2a08955a980c: Memory hook: Five carried one: Shenzhou five, Yang Liwei, two thousand three.
china/china-space.2514a50d24d2: Drag the slider to travel from Dongfanghong one to today, or press. The top row shows the big missions; the bars underneath show how many rockets China launched each year, approximate.
china/china-space.ef385bc75d9b: Don’t mix up: Shenzhou one was uncrewed. The first crewed Shenzhou was number five.
