earth/earth-layers.b735a09cbac0: Inner core. A solid ball of iron and nickel at the center. A solid ball about one thousand two hundred twenty kilometers in radius, about seventy percent the size of the Moon. About five thousand two hundred degrees Celsius, roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun. It stays solid because the pressure is about three point six million times the air pressure at sea level. The densest layer: about thirteen grams per cubic centimeter, more than four times as dense as crust rock.
earth/earth-layers.06332b3ddbba: Roughly one hundred to three hundred fifty kilometers below the surface, in the upper mantle.
earth/earth-layers.ae06baa86188: The real thing. An iron meteorite found at Toluca, Mexico. Scientists think Earth’s core is made of iron-nickel metal much like this. Found at Toluca, Mexico
earth/earth-layers.479a0702d4ab: A solid ball about one thousand two hundred twenty kilometers in radius, about seventy percent the size of the Moon.
earth/earth-layers.a999e83a5221: The mantle-core boundary at two thousand nine hundred kilometers is called the Gutenberg discontinuity.
earth/earth-layers.b91e01d3ed6f: The deepest hole ever drilled is about twelve kilometers. How do scientists know about the core?
earth/earth-layers.f096cc25cd41: The densest layer: about thirteen grams per cubic centimeter, more than four times as dense as crust rock.
earth/earth-layers.8b085e5b2d98: Supports GSE S six E five A: ask questions to compare and contrast the crust, mantle, inner and outer core, including temperature, density, thickness and composition. Suggested flow: one, use the Cutaway slider and the “Journey to the core” story to meet each layer; two, have students drag the drill and record temperature, pressure and density at several depths, then graph them and describe the pattern;
earth/earth-layers.337d32590073: About thirty to seventy kilometers thick, thickest under high mountains.
earth/earth-layers.98f7ac83dd00: about one thousand two hundred twenty kilometers in radius
earth/earth-layers.842090536883: A tiny fraction may be melted, about one percent, which helps it flow.
earth/earth-layers.6dcc53db99a4: Oceanic crust. Thin, dense rock under the oceans. Only about five to ten kilometers thick. Made of dark basalt, which has more iron and magnesium. Denser than continental crust, so it sinks beneath it when the two collide. Oceanic crust has a density of about three point zero grams per cubic centimeter. Young: almost none is older than about two hundred million years, because old ocean floor sinks back into the mantle.
earth/earth-layers.abbb0603b057: Some continental rocks are about four billion years old.
earth/earth-layers.bea3bfbf5b52: Mantle. The thickest layer: hot, solid, slowly moving rock. The whole mantle is about two thousand nine hundred kilometers thick and makes up about eighty-four percent of Earth’s volume. Solid rock rich in iron and magnesium, peridotite in the upper part. Temperature rises from about one thousand degrees Celsius near the top to about three thousand seven hundred degrees Celsius at the bottom. Hot rock slowly rises and cooler rock sinks. These convection currents help move the plates. The mantle-core boundary at two thousand nine hundred kilometers is called the Gutenberg discontinuity.
earth/earth-layers.26e68e34908d: Denser than continental crust, with a density of about three point zero grams per cubic centimeter, so it sinks beneath it when the two collide.

earth/fossils-time.fe8211aa5e5a: Layer seven, Cenozoic sandstone. Petrified wood and insect in amber. The YOUNGEST layer: it is on top. Petrified wood: minerals replaced the wood cell by cell, keeping even the tree rings. Amber is hardened tree resin. An insect trapped in sticky resin can be preserved whole: a preserved-remains fossil. Other ways to keep original remains: freezing in ice, woolly mammoths, or sinking into tar pits.
earth/fossils-time.3b189be35f15: The dike is fifty million years old, so layer six must be older than fifty million years and layer seven younger.
earth/fossils-time.010efa465a85: Layer one, Cambrian shale. Trilobites, molds and casts. The OLDEST layer here: it is at the bottom, law of superposition. Trilobites were sea animals with hard, jointed shells, distant relatives of insects and crabs. They are extinct. Many are preserved as molds, the hollow print left when the shell dissolved, and casts, the mold later filled with minerals. Shale forms from fine mud settling in calm water, so this place was once a sea floor.
earth/fossils-time.f462e88a37f2: Note: the three D block is a teaching composite; real places rarely show every age in one spot, and ages are approximate. Common misconceptions: humans lived alongside dinosaurs; every dead organism becomes a fossil; a fossil is the original bone.
earth/fossils-time.c61c8aabc5e1: Layer six, Cretaceous chalk. Ammonites, index fossils. Chalk is made of the shells of microscopic sea plankton. Ammonites were squid-like animals with coiled shells. Each species lived for a short time but spread widely, so they make excellent index fossils. The sea returned! High sea levels flooded much of North America at this time. The Cretaceous ended sixty-six million years ago with a mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs, except birds, and the ammonites.
earth/fossils-time.2b1bb7162a17: The real thing. A petrified log in Petrified Forest National Park. Minerals slowly replaced the wood, so the tree is now solid stone. These trees grew more than two hundred million years ago, in the Triassic: petrified wood forms in rocks of many ages, and this log is much older than layer seven. Arizona, USA
earth/fossils-time.be2b909decc0: The real thing. Dinosaur trackways in Portugal. Long lines of footprints from giant sauropods were pressed into mud that later hardened into rock. Serra de Aire, Portugal
earth/fossils-time.465002b77ef1: Layer four, Carboniferous coal and shale
earth/fossils-time.0ceffd4d21b0: The real thing. An ammonite fossil in the Natural History Museum, London. Ammonites were sea animals with coiled shells, relatives of today’s squid. Natural History Museum, London
earth/fossils-time.952a5e014e79: Layer two, Ordovician limestone. Brachiopod shells and crinoid stems. Limestone forms in warm, shallow seas from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures. Brachiopods look like clams but are a different group of shelled animals. Crinoids, “sea lilies”, are animals related to starfish. Their stems break into little disc-shaped pieces. Climate clue: warm-sea fossils on dry land show that the surface and climate here have changed.
earth/fossils-time.3ab5d99440ed: Layer three, Devonian sandstone. Fish bones, petrified. The Devonian is called the “Age of Fishes”. The fish was buried quickly in sand. Minerals in groundwater filled the tiny spaces in its bones and turned them to stone, petrification. Sandstone forms from sand on beaches, in rivers or in deserts.
earth/fossils-time.59c8204c606f: Layer four, Carboniferous coal and shale. Fern leaves, carbon films. Coal formed from huge swamp forests of giant ferns and tree-sized club mosses. Pressed leaves left a thin black film of carbon: a carbon-film fossil. Climate clue: coal has even been found in Antarctica, so that land was once warm and swampy, and in a different place.
earth/fossils-time.0aa3946e430b: Nobody ever saw a living dinosaur, so how do we know they died out millions of years before the first humans? Rock layers are a history book written in stone, with the oldest page at the bottom. Peel back the three D rock layers below, find the fossils hidden inside, and watch how an ammonite becomes a fossil!
earth/fossils-time.0cbf8b4fc2e5: The fossils hidden in the three D layers are drawings. These are real ones, found in real rock. Click a photo to enlarge it.
earth/fossils-time.9588d0b702aa: The real thing. Leaves of a seed fern pressed into rock in the Late Carboniferous, when swampy forests covered what is now Ohio. The fern is Neuropteris. Northeastern Ohio, USA
earth/fossils-time.c802fbe8f4c1: Layer five, Jurassic red sandstone. Dinosaur footprints, trace fossils. Dig away the layers above to see three-toed dinosaur tracks on the top of this layer. Footprints are trace fossils: evidence of what an animal did, not of its body. Burrows, nests and fossil dung, coprolites, are trace fossils too. Tracks show how an animal walked, how fast it moved and whether it travelled in groups. The red color comes from iron oxide, often a clue to a hot climate with dry seasons.
earth/fossils-time.71d4719052fa: The real thing. The bony head armour of Dunkleosteus, a giant fish of the Devonian Period, the “Age of Fishes”. Its fossils come from rocks in Ohio that are about three hundred sixty million years old. Late Devonian
earth/fossils-time.edbc8b9ded9d: The Mesozoic is called the Age of Reptiles. It lasted from two hundred fifty-two to sixty-six million years ago.
earth/fossils-time.356fba4ca225: Common mix-up: Trilobites are not insects or dinosaurs. They died out about two hundred fifty million years ago, before the first dinosaurs.
earth/fossils-time.ab72bdcd6e23: Supports GSE S six E five, especially S six E five F: explain how fossils show evidence of Earth’s changing surface and climate, and use the law of superposition to find the relative ages of rock layers and fossils. Suggested use: have students dig layer by layer with the slider and name the environment each layer’s fossils point to, sea, swamp, desert, sea.
earth/fossils-time.99603d41c43d: Igneous dike, intrusion. No fossils: it was molten rock. Magma squeezed up through a crack and cooled into a wall of igneous rock. It cuts through layers one to six, so it is YOUNGER than all of them, cross-cutting relationships. Layer seven lies on top of it, so layer seven is younger still. Igneous rock can be dated in years using radioactive elements that decay at a steady rate, half-life. This is absolute dating. The dike is fifty million years old, so layer six must be older than fifty million years and layer seven younger.
earth/fossils-time.96a286385d73: The geologic time scale: a four point six billion-year journey
earth/fossils-time.ae703ffcec7b: It cuts through layers one to six, so it is YOUNGER than all of them, cross-cutting relationships. Layer seven lies on top of it, so layer seven is younger still.
earth/fossils-time.53564055f4e3: Common mix-up: Humans never lived alongside non-bird dinosaurs: about sixty-six million years separate them.
earth/fossils-time.0c1a58b84820: The Precambrian, about eighty-eight percent of Earth’s history
earth/fossils-time.dfc63d77e0a9: Drag the slider through Earth’s history. If all of Earth’s history were squeezed into one twenty-four-hour day, when would humans show up?
earth/fossils-time.97d252a729c8: Then click the dike and ask what “the dike is fifty million years old” tells us about layers six and seven, combining relative and absolute dating.
earth/fossils-time.3a6fb324c438: The real thing. This trilobite lived about five hundred five million years ago, in the Cambrian. It is Elrathia kingii. Its fossil was found in shale from the Wheeler Formation in Utah. Rock about three point four centimeters across
earth/fossils-time.4d2735572799: The Cretaceous ended sixty-six million years ago with a mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs and the ammonites. Among the dinosaurs, birds were the exception.

earth/natural-resources.2fab49b12163: Wind power. Moving air spins turbines. Wind spins the giant blades, which turn a generator inside the nacelle at the top of the tower. Wind exists because the Sun heats Earth unevenly, so wind energy is really solar energy too. Power rises quickly with wind speed. Below about three meters per second the blades barely turn. Try the Wind slider!
earth/natural-resources.2a60e1750a6e: Supports GSE S six E six A and S six E six B. For the first, renewable or sustainable energy resources such as hydro, solar, wind, geothermal, tidal and biomass versus nonrenewable resources such as nuclear and fossil fuels, and how they are used in everyday life. The nonrenewable examples are uranium for nuclear and oil, coal and natural gas for fossil fuels. For the second, design and evaluate solutions for sustaining energy resources: conservation, reduce, reuse, recycle.
earth/natural-resources.98613d7443e6: It releases lots of C O two
earth/natural-resources.ec57838bb492: Burning coal releases the most C O two of any fuel, plus pollution that causes smog and acid rain. Mining scars the land.
earth/natural-resources.7f8fa31ec0de: If the power went out in your town tonight, what would stop working first, and where does that electricity come from anyway? Turning on a light, charging a phone, riding the bus: everything needs energy. Click the power plants in the three D town below to see where their energy comes from and whether it can be replaced, then design an energy plan that keeps the town powered day and night.
earth/natural-resources.0f8d0feca74f: Biomass. Energy stored in living things. Wood, crop waste, manure and fuels made from corn or sugarcane, ethanol, can be burned for heat or electricity. Plants store the Sun’s energy through photosynthesis, so biomass is stored solar energy. It is renewable only if we replant as fast as we use it. Burning it still releases C O two and smoke.
earth/natural-resources.ce0b3d043151: The real thing. The Turów open-pit coal mine in Poland, with its power station behind. Coal is dug here and burned next door to make electricity. Lower Silesia, Poland
earth/natural-resources.4e4774114f39: The real thing. A pumpjack lifting oil out of a well in the Permian Basin near Monahans, Texas, one of the most productive oil regions in the United States. Texas, USA
earth/natural-resources.ccf5189dd459: The real thing. Rows of solar panels at the Travers Solar Farm. The panels are photovoltaic. Each panel turns sunlight straight into electricity. Alberta, Canada
earth/natural-resources.ad94e91435c1: Efficiency means getting the same job done with less energy: LED bulbs use about seventy-five percent less electricity than old bulbs.
earth/natural-resources.d0fa7c60ae2a: The real thing. Cooling towers of the Kalinin nuclear power plant. The white plume is water vapor, not smoke. Russia
earth/natural-resources.8b39dabe4c96: The real thing. Hoover Dam on the Colorado River. Water stored behind the dam falls through turbines to make hydroelectric power. Nevada-Arizona border, USA
earth/natural-resources.b781daf49a4d: Coal, oil and natural gas store sunlight captured by living things millions of years ago. Look at the rock layers on the front of the three D model: a black coal seam, plus oil and gas trapped under a cap rock.
earth/natural-resources.e522bfe0a243: It is renewable only if we replant as fast as we use it. Burning it still releases C O two and smoke.
earth/natural-resources.1de48357d1d0: About three hundred million years ago, huge swamp forests and ocean plankton captured the Sun’s energy by photosynthesis, the forests for coal and the plankton for oil and gas.
earth/natural-resources.860fb6ab8edd: Power rises quickly with wind speed. Below about three meters per second the blades barely turn. Try the Wind slider!
earth/natural-resources.8b84729fd855: Natural gas. Gaseous fossil fuel, often found with oil. Natural gas, mostly methane, forms the same way as oil and collects above it in the trap, because gas is lighter. It heats homes, fuels stoves and runs power plants. Pipelines carry it across the country. It releases about half the C O two of coal when burned, but methane that leaks is a powerful greenhouse gas.
earth/natural-resources.ab31e35b09da: Reduce, reuse, recycle: making new things from recycled aluminum uses about ninety-five percent less energy than making them from raw ore.
earth/natural-resources.9db9a404cea0: It makes no C O two while running, and a small amount of fuel makes a lot of energy.
earth/natural-resources.4f0dda33a526: The little power plants in the three D town are models. These are real ones, and some are enormous. Click a photo to enlarge it; the video never starts by itself.
earth/natural-resources.a244898a2c73: Hydro is limited to two hundred megawatts: there is only one river. Batteries supply power at night, but only if there is enough solar to charge them in the day.
earth/natural-resources.d4d24b6a5564: Coal. Fossil fuel from ancient swamp plants. Coal formed from plants in swamps about three hundred million years ago that were buried, squeezed and heated over millions of years. Power plants burn coal to boil water; the steam spins turbines. See the black coal seam in the rock layers. Burning coal releases the most C O two of any fuel, plus pollution that causes smog and acid rain. Mining scars the land.
earth/natural-resources.0a99832b5dfb: The town needs one thousand megawatts in the day and seven hundred megawatts at night, with megawatts abbreviated M W. Mix energy sources with the sliders so the lights stay on in all four weather cases, while keeping C O two and cost low. Hint: solar makes nothing at night, wind makes little when it is calm, and batteries can store daytime solar power for the night.
earth/natural-resources.c02051f410a7: Burning which fuel releases the most C O two for the same energy?
earth/natural-resources.58ba799a770a: Your town: saving energy. The cheapest energy is the energy you don’t use. Conservation means using less: turn off lights, unplug chargers, walk, bike or share rides. Efficiency means getting the same job done with less energy: LED bulbs use about seventy-five percent less electricity than old bulbs. Reduce, reuse, recycle: making new things from recycled aluminum uses about ninety-five percent less energy than making them from raw ore.
earth/natural-resources.1d3085419096: Memory hint: Water cycle and gravity equals hydro.
earth/natural-resources.90a114a0d6d6: Coal formed from plants in swamps about three hundred million years ago that were buried, squeezed and heated over millions of years.
earth/natural-resources.9a33509c55e6: The real thing. Wood pellets, a biomass fuel made from pressed sawdust. Burning them releases energy that trees stored from sunlight.
earth/natural-resources.247362e940e8: Note: planner numbers are simplified approximations for comparison, for example, coal about one metric ton of C O two per megawatt-hour, natural gas about zero point four five metric tons.
earth/natural-resources.26d384692416: Nuclear power. Splitting uranium atoms. In the reactor, uranium atoms split, nuclear fission, and release huge amounts of heat, which boils water to spin turbines. It makes no C O two while running, and a small amount of fuel makes a lot of energy. It is nonrenewable because uranium is a mined metal that will run out. The used fuel stays radioactive for thousands of years and must be stored safely.
earth/natural-resources.5df8dfd7fb1f: It releases about half the C O two of coal when burned, but methane that leaks is a powerful greenhouse gas.

earth/oceans.d4b1bae4821c: Continental slope. The steep drop from the shelf to the deep sea. It marks the true edge of the continent. The depth drops from about two hundred meters to three thousand to four thousand meters. Underwater avalanches of sediment carve deep submarine canyons into it.
earth/oceans.e062b4264023: On average, one kilogram of seawater holds about thirty-five grams of salt, three point five percent, mostly sodium chloride. Hot, dry seas with lots of evaporation, like the Red Sea, are saltier; river mouths and melting ice make water fresher.
earth/oceans.c0ce1d8492fd: The real thing. A “black smoker” on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Scalding, mineral-rich water shoots out of the sea floor where the plates pull apart. Three thousand three hundred meters under water, or about two miles
earth/oceans.991b45d6712b: The highest point of a wave is the blank and the lowest point is the blank.
earth/oceans.f330e8f4f0a5: The real thing. A map of sea-floor depth, bathymetry, around the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific. The long, curved groove is the trench; its deepest point, the Challenger Deep, is about eleven thousand meters down. Western Pacific Ocean
earth/oceans.7714d808eef5: The longest mountain range on Earth, about sixty-five thousand kilometers long, winding through every ocean.
earth/oceans.99acad54aaee: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is about eleven thousand meters deep. Mount Everest would fit inside with room to spare.
earth/oceans.66b69821f95e: Supports GSE S six E three: the significant role of water in Earth processes, including ocean composition, salinity, ocean-floor topography — shelf, slope, abyssal plain, trench, mid-ocean ridge — and the causes of waves, currents and tides. Suggested use: run the Sea-floor dive story and have students sketch a simple profile.
earth/oceans.d3d67c13f163: The Mariana Trench is about eleven thousand meters deep.
earth/oceans.d260736ef97f: Memory hint: Seamount equals sea and mountain.
earth/oceans.21357a9b19f5: Where is the longest mountain range on Earth? Hint: almost all of it is under water. Oceans cover about seventy-one percent of Earth’s surface and hide mountain ranges longer, and canyons deeper, than any on land. Dive across the three D sea floor, then switch to the globe to see warm and cold currents circle the world!
earth/oceans.69ddd079d3a5: Mid-ocean ridge. An underwater mountain chain where new sea floor forms. The longest mountain range on Earth, about sixty-five thousand kilometers long, winding through every ocean. Plates pull apart here, a divergent boundary. Magma rises into the central rift valley and cools into new ocean crust: sea-floor spreading. Rock gets older the farther it is from the ridge. Iceland is a piece of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that rises above sea level.
earth/oceans.3f59511099c9: Continental shelf. The shallow, gently sloping edge of a continent. The flooded edge of a continent, usually less than about two hundred meters deep. Sunlight reaches much of it, so it is rich in sea life and holds most of the world’s fishing grounds. Oil and natural gas are often drilled here. During ice ages, sea level was lower and much of the shelf was dry land.
earth/oceans.01379c3f5aaa: Seamount. An underwater volcanic mountain. A volcano that rises at least one thousand meters above the sea floor but does not reach the surface. A seamount whose top was flattened by waves when it was near the surface is called a guyot. Seamounts are hot spots for fish, corals and other life.
earth/oceans.d1b460d474d3: The depth drops from about two hundred meters to between three thousand and four thousand meters.
earth/oceans.03c9772a26ac: Ocean trench. The deepest part of the ocean. A long, narrow, very deep valley where one plate sinks beneath another, subduction. The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is about eleven thousand meters deep. Mount Everest would fit inside with room to spare. Strong earthquakes and tsunamis often start near trenches.
earth/oceans.6ac534d0101a: One of the flattest places on Earth, about four thousand to six thousand meters deep.
earth/oceans.010670a353ca: About thirty-five grams of salt per kilogram, three point five percent
earth/oceans.46ec9fba19fa: A volcano that rises at least one thousand meters above the sea floor but does not reach the surface.
earth/oceans.fe5fa0e6db98: The real thing. The Great Barrier Reef off Queensland, Australia, from the air. The world’s largest coral reef system grows in the warm, shallow, sunlit water of the continental shelf. Queensland, Australia
earth/oceans.a612d969caf2: Abyssal plain. The flat, deep ocean floor. One of the flattest places on Earth, about four thousand to six thousand meters deep. Covered by a thick blanket of fine mud and the tiny shells of plankton that sank from above. Totally dark and near freezing, yet strange animals still live here.
earth/oceans.02c7b8ce049a: The flooded edge of a continent, usually less than about two hundred meters deep.
earth/oceans.5356a1994c31: Near Greenland and Antarctica, seawater becomes very cold and salty — freezing sea ice leaves its salt behind — so it grows denser and sinks, then creeps along the sea floor around the world. One full loop takes about one thousand years!

earth/plate-tectonics.9538894ae913: Transform fault. A crack where plates grind sideways past each other. The plates slide horizontally in opposite directions. Crust is neither created nor destroyed here. California’s San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary: the Pacific plate moves northwest about three to five centimeters per year relative to North America. Most transform faults are short offsets connecting pieces of mid-ocean ridges.
earth/plate-tectonics.5f86e0dca3c0: Strong: can destroy buildings in a city. Earthquakes this size, same whole number: about one hundred thirty per year worldwide. Each plus one in magnitude means about thirty-two times the energy and ten times the seismograph swing, with the energy factor being ten to the power of one point five, about thirty-one point six.
earth/plate-tectonics.eaf07fccd813: Because old ocean floor keeps sinking, none is older than about two hundred million years.
earth/plate-tectonics.4e0327ed4de4: Ring of Fire. Belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific. A horseshoe-shaped belt about forty thousand kilometers long around the Pacific Ocean. About seventy-five percent of Earth’s active volcanoes and about ninety percent of its earthquakes happen here. It follows subduction zones where Pacific Ocean plates sink under the plates around them.
earth/plate-tectonics.215052b82cef: The two continents squeeze d closer, so the crust thickens and the mountains rise. Shortcut: one centimeter per year for one million years equals ten kilometers. Drag the time slider in the three D view.
earth/plate-tectonics.64bb32856e87: The Atlantic began to open about one hundred eighty million years ago. At two point five centimeters per year that gives about four thousand five hundred kilometers, the same size as the real ocean, several thousand kilometers. Shortcut: one centimeter per year for one million years equals ten kilometers.
earth/plate-tectonics.893a79e375c1: Why didn't people believe him? Wegener could not explain what force moved the continents. Only in the nineteen sixties, when scientists discovered seafloor spreading and magnetic stripes, was plate tectonics widely accepted.
earth/plate-tectonics.daf46dd40d5d: Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading in the early nineteen sixties, and the stripes proved it.
earth/plate-tectonics.8af484fc438b: Common mix-up: The sinking plate does not melt right at the trench. Melting happens about one hundred kilometers deep, under the volcanoes.
earth/plate-tectonics.2f8493fee564: Mid-ocean ridge. Underwater mountain range where plates pull apart. The longest mountain range on Earth: about sixty-five thousand kilometers long, almost all underwater. Magma rises into the crack, cools and becomes new basalt seafloor. A rift valley runs along the crest of the ridge. Iceland is a piece of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that rises above sea level.
earth/plate-tectonics.f9f4fface897: In nineteen twelve Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift: about three hundred to two hundred million years ago all continents were joined in one supercontinent, Pangaea, “all lands”. Drag the continents back into place, then switch on the evidence layers and see whether fossils, mountains and glacier scratches line up!
earth/plate-tectonics.6e22c0ab4bf5: The real thing. An anticline: rock layers that were once flat, squeezed sideways until they arched upward. Round Top Hill, Maryland, USA
earth/plate-tectonics.2e52b2e5e039: The Mariana Trench is the deepest place on Earth, about eleven thousand meters deep.
earth/plate-tectonics.42e5767f1d2a: The road across the fault is offset by d. Shortcut: one centimeter per year for one million years equals ten kilometers. Drag the time slider in the three D view.
earth/plate-tectonics.d7b78c3461f0: Earthquakes. Sudden shaking when rocks slip. Rocks along a boundary lock together. Stress builds until they slip suddenly, releasing energy as seismic waves. The point underground where slipping starts is the focus; the spot on the surface right above it is the epicenter. Earthquakes happen at all three kinds of boundaries; the deepest, down to about seven hundred kilometers, happen along sinking plates.
earth/plate-tectonics.6506f479b669: Two to ten centimeters per year, like fingernails growing
earth/plate-tectonics.198c00a35d88: Seafloor spreading. The ocean floor grows outward from the ridge. New crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides like two conveyor belts. Rock is youngest at the ridge and gets older farther away. Earth’s magnetic field flips every so often. Cooling lava records it, leaving matching magnetic stripes on both sides of the ridge. Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading in the early nineteen sixties, and the stripes proved it.
earth/plate-tectonics.e547388d63d8: The ocean between the plates widens by d, each side moves away from the ridge by half of it. Shortcut: one centimeter per year for one million years equals ten kilometers. Drag the time slider in the three D view.
earth/plate-tectonics.e1e553a27cbe: Earth’s lithosphere is broken into about fifteen major plates. Most volcanoes and earthquakes line up along plate boundaries. The volcanoes are shown as triangles and the earthquakes as dots. Click a line, a volcano or a dot.
earth/plate-tectonics.e6d9fc245306: Georgia connection: About three hundred million years ago, ancient Africa collided with North America while Pangaea was forming. The collision pushed up the Appalachian Mountains, including north Georgia’s Blue Ridge. Erosion has worn them low and rounded since then.
earth/plate-tectonics.e7f6b8dc7d38: Who proposed the idea of continental drift in nineteen twelve?
earth/plate-tectonics.e8f36fe21a14: Note: the three D models exaggerate height and compress time enormously; boundaries on the world map are simplified sketch lines.
earth/plate-tectonics.2c11b13e4165: Ocean trench. Deepest valleys in the ocean, where a plate dives down. Forms where an oceanic plate bends and sinks beneath another plate. The Mariana Trench is the deepest place on Earth, about eleven thousand meters deep. Trenches form long curved lines around the Pacific Ocean.
earth/plate-tectonics.ab0411bee4ab: Oceanic plate. Thin, dense plate under the ocean. Its crust is dark basalt, only about five to ten kilometers thick. Denser than a continental plate, so it sinks, subducts, when the two collide. Because old ocean floor keeps sinking, none is older than about two hundred million years.
earth/plate-tectonics.0408e390a37b: Its crust is granite-like rock, thirty to seventy kilometers thick.
earth/plate-tectonics.5cbc9e52041f: Continental plate. Thick, light plate that carries land. Its crust is granite-like rock, thirty to seventy kilometers thick. Too light, buoyant, to sink far into the mantle. When two continental plates collide, the crust crumples upward into huge mountains.
earth/plate-tectonics.9f4cab262cdd: The real thing. Wallace Creek makes a sharp zigzag where it crosses the San Andreas Fault. Earthquake after earthquake has dragged the stream bed sideways. Stream offset about one hundred thirty meters, four hundred thirty feet
earth/plate-tectonics.02da289508c0: Folded mountains. The tallest mountains, built by colliding continents. Neither continental plate sinks, so the crust crumples, folds and stacks up, growing thick and tall. India has been pushing into Asia for about fifty million years, building the Himalayas and Mount Everest, eight thousand eight hundred forty-nine meters. The Himalayas are still rising by a few millimeters each year. The Appalachian Mountains, including north Georgia’s Blue Ridge, formed in an ancient continental collision about three hundred million years ago.
earth/plate-tectonics.be26f0cbfe0d: The real thing. Þingvellir, Thingvellir, Iceland: a rift valley that marks the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Here a divergent boundary rises above the sea, so you can walk through it. Southwestern Iceland
earth/plate-tectonics.e46bacd64b02: The Appalachian Mountains, including north Georgia’s Blue Ridge, formed in an ancient continental collision about three hundred million years ago.
earth/plate-tectonics.8ba6fdfd9c8d: Supports GSE S six E five F: construct an explanation of how the movement of lithospheric plates causes major geologic events such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, including convergent, divergent and transform boundaries. This movement is called plate tectonics. Ideas: one, in each three D boundary mode, have students predict what will form before dragging the time slider;
earth/plate-tectonics.dca8e18fa592: The longest mountain range on Earth: about sixty-five thousand kilometers long, almost all underwater.
earth/plate-tectonics.2ea1d87066e3: The real thing. The San Andreas Fault from the air: the long straight scar running across the Carrizo Plain is where two plates grind past each other. Carrizo Plain, California, USA
earth/plate-tectonics.78af2a948d45: The real thing. Mount Saint Helens erupting on May eighteenth, nineteen eighty. It is one of the Cascade volcanoes, which sit above a subduction zone. Washington State, USA
earth/plate-tectonics.e1fb7de7c79f: Earthquakes happen at all three kinds of boundaries; the deepest happen along sinking plates, down to about seven hundred kilometers.
earth/plate-tectonics.05e1b6f3823a: Memory hint: Continent and continent equals crumple, like pushing a rug against a wall.
earth/plate-tectonics.b8c4d9901530: The ocean plate slides d under the continent: that much seafloor sinks back into the mantle. Shortcut: one centimeter per year for one million years equals ten kilometers. Drag the time slider in the three D view.
earth/plate-tectonics.a7957dfc3b6c: India has been pushing into Asia for about fifty million years, building the Himalayas and Mount Everest, eight thousand eight hundred forty-nine meters.
earth/plate-tectonics.4b53ccf7a42b: About seventy-five percent of Earth’s active volcanoes and about ninety percent of its earthquakes happen here.
earth/plate-tectonics.9d727c9eae9f: California’s San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary: the Pacific plate moves northwest about three to five centimeters per year relative to North America.
earth/plate-tectonics.ad5342a81489: The three D blocks above are simplified. These are the real places. Click a photo to enlarge it; the video never starts by itself.
earth/plate-tectonics.1a38d0d8c380: Three seismograph stations recorded the same earthquake. P waves arrive first, at about six kilometers per second. S waves later, at about three point five kilometers per second. Use the gap to get each station’s distance: d is about eight point four times the S minus P gap in seconds, with d in kilometers. Then tap the map where the quake happened.
earth/plate-tectonics.c6fa959d2a1a: The real thing. The Himalaya seen from the International Space Station: the crumpled crust where India is still pushing into Asia. Seen from about four hundred kilometers up, about two hundred fifty miles
earth/plate-tectonics.3e3b6252f67e: GPS did not exist in nineteen twelve. Today GPS shows plates moving a few centimeters per year, supporting plate tectonics.
earth/plate-tectonics.cba37145bfed: Its crust is dark basalt, only about five to ten kilometers thick.
earth/plate-tectonics.2f033b87db51: A horseshoe-shaped belt about forty thousand kilometers long around the Pacific Ocean.

earth/rocks-minerals.e6d7b189db4c: The three D rock cycle shows where rocks form. These are real specimens you could hold in your hand. Click a photo to enlarge it; the video never starts by itself.
earth/rocks-minerals.2e202b6fe5da: Fine-grained: crystals smaller than about one millimeter, basalt. Typical of lava flows at the surface: extrusive rock. Twice as big, about four times as long to cool.
earth/rocks-minerals.292680a1a32e: The real thing. Sandstone pillars of Tianzi Mountain in the Wulingyuan area of Zhangjiajie, Hunan, China. Water and ice wore the rock away along its cracks until only these tall columns were left. Zhangjiajie, Hunan, China
earth/rocks-minerals.35bda26f56c2: Deep underground it is hot enough for rock to melt into magma, about seven hundred to one thousand three hundred degrees Celsius.
earth/rocks-minerals.668229ca0a85: The real thing. Sandstone: sand grains, mostly quartz, pressed and cemented together into rock. Fine-grained: each grain is smaller than a pinhead
earth/rocks-minerals.51de3279bda7: Supports GSE S six E five B, plan and carry out an investigation of the characteristics of minerals and how minerals contribute to rock composition, and S six E five C, explain how to classify rocks by their formation and how rocks change through geologic processes in the rock cycle. Ideas: one, use the three D “grain’s journey” slider and have students name the process at each stage;
earth/rocks-minerals.f81aceb0c002: Memory hint: Squeeze and glue: compaction and cementation.
earth/rocks-minerals.d791f29d604a: between two point five and ten
earth/rocks-minerals.a7c5058eea93: between six point five and ten
earth/rocks-minerals.7173d7e96b5d: Sedimentary rock: sediment is compacted and cemented, in the top few kilometers. Most places heat up by about twenty-five to thirty degrees Celsius per kilometer; near magma it can be much more.
earth/rocks-minerals.13ca553a7e9b: Magma and melting. Rock melts deep underground. Deep underground it is hot enough for rock to melt into magma, at about seven hundred to one thousand three hundred degrees Celsius. Magma is less dense than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises. Any rock type, igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic, can melt and start the cycle again.
earth/rocks-minerals.3c981f0ebf51: Glass has a hardness of about five point five. Which mineral can scratch it?
earth/rocks-minerals.4543f53dd083: Melting begins! With some water, granite-type rock starts to melt at about six hundred fifty to seven hundred degrees Celsius—magma. Most places heat up by about twenty-five to thirty degrees Celsius per kilometer; near magma it can be much more.
earth/rocks-minerals.88d14ed74ce7: between three point five and ten
earth/rocks-minerals.d366720a53de: The real thing. Granite from Rhode Island. Magma cooled slowly deep underground, so the crystals had time to grow big enough to see. Westerly, Rhode Island, USA
earth/rocks-minerals.7aab233bdab7: The real thing. Garnet gneiss from the Adirondack Mountains, cut and polished. Heat and pressure deep in the crust squeezed its minerals into bands. Specimen fifteen centimeters wide, six inches
earth/rocks-minerals.9244874ababd: between five point five and ten
earth/rocks-minerals.9d821e8cafc6: Low-grade metamorphism: shale, slate. Most places heat up by about twenty-five to thirty degrees Celsius per kilometer; near magma it can be much more.
earth/rocks-minerals.9ff5cdabd570: The real thing. The Stone Forest in Yunnan, China, also called Shilin: tall pillars of limestone, a sedimentary rock. Rainwater is slightly acidic; over a very long time it dissolved the rock along cracks and left these stone “trees” standing. Shilin, Yunnan, China
earth/rocks-minerals.2a217f793693: Coarse-grained: crystals from a few millimeters to over one centimeter, granite. Big magma bodies deep underground, like Georgia’s Stone Mountain: intrusive rock. Twice as big, about four times as long to cool.
earth/rocks-minerals.bd2ff9d848e4: The real thing. Basalt from northeastern California. Lava cooled quickly at the surface; the holes are bubbles of volcanic gas trapped as it hardened. Specimen eight centimeters across, three inches

earth/soil.5de2e98e3819: Two point five centimeters of topsoil can take hundreds of years. Older soils have more, clearer layers.
earth/soil.0fe9c87b97bd: Only about five percent, but it holds water, feeds plants and glues grains into crumbs.
earth/soil.8e5780e0ca1e: About how much of a healthy soil’s volume is pore space, air and water?
earth/soil.b6b997be0067: The real thing. Lichen growing on bare rock. Lichens are among the first living things to settle on rock, and they slowly help break it down, the first step toward soil. Shawnee National Forest, Illinois, USA
earth/soil.357eea06769f: Supports GSE S six E five, especially S six E five E: develop a model of how natural processes and human activity change rocks and Earth’s surface. The natural processes are weathering, erosion, and deposition. Soil is made of weathered rock and decomposed organic material. Suggested use: drag the Soil age slider from zero to one hundred and have students predict which horizon appears first and last—C first, O and B last.
earth/soil.a6f99102ab59: How long does nature need to make a layer of soil as thick as your thumb? Hint: far longer than you have been alive. Soil is not “just dirt”. It is a mix of weathered rock, decayed living things, air and water, and it takes hundreds to thousands of years to form. Dig into the three D soil profile below, click each layer, and watch soil build up step by step!
earth/soil.a4cd5b04a33f: Water and air together fill about half the volume of soil. Click an ingredient.
earth/soil.5b6c713b3190: Set the sand and clay percentages—the rest is silt—or tap the triangle. Your soil appears as a fifth tube in the lab above.
earth/soil.6bbcad376bd6: Air and water in pores. About half of soil is open space! A healthy soil is about forty-five percent minerals, five percent organic matter, twenty-five percent water and twenty-five percent air. Water and air fill the spaces, pores, between grains. Roots and soil animals need both. Permeability is how easily water flows through soil: fast through sand, slow through clay. Watch the rain: water slows down in the clay-rich B horizon and collects above the bedrock as groundwater.
earth/soil.134bf225bb51: The real thing. Roots hold soil in place. Around this old tree stump the bare soil has been washed away, but the soil gripped by its roots still stands up like a little table. Near Charters Towers, Queensland, Australia
earth/soil.e70c0161c08e: Roughly twenty-five percent water and twenty-five percent air, with forty-five percent minerals and five percent organic matter.
earth/soil.d837134be548: Soil equals weathered rock particles, humus, water, and air. Humus is decayed organic matter. Click each ingredient to learn more.
earth/soil.b4a96cc1e734: The real thing. A forest floor covered with fallen leaves and small mushrooms. This litter is the O horizon; fungi are already turning it into humus. Potawatomi State Park, Wisconsin, USA
earth/soil.7fa020220722: The real thing. Earthworm burrows in a column of soil after twenty-eight days. These tunnels are pathways for air and water.
earth/soil.986de40252c7: A horizon, topsoil. The richest, most alive layer. A mix of humus and small mineral grains, sand, silt and clay. Humus makes it dark. Most plant roots, earthworms and microorganisms live here. Farmers grow crops in topsoil. Forming just two point five centimeters of it can take hundreds of years. Some soils have a pale E layer under A, where water has washed minerals out.
earth/soil.48a9c8d1b938: The three D profile is tidy. Real soil is messier and more alive. Click a photo to enlarge it.
earth/soil.630a20479cac: The real thing. A real soil profile dug near Raleigh, North Carolina. Can you see where one layer ends and the next begins? This soil has a clay-rich subsoil, B horizon. Near Raleigh, North Carolina, USA
earth/soil.9ee04dfe71de: The real thing. An earthworm found just under the soil surface. Worms eat dead plant material and mix it into the soil.
earth/soil.ca4f43543c74: Farmers grow crops in topsoil. Forming just two point five centimeters of it can take hundreds of years.
earth/soil.eeaab93291c9: USDA soil texture triangle: twelve soil classes by their percentages of sand, silt and clay. Infiltration and water-holding numbers are typical values for each class, approximate.
earth/soil.236fa8419585: A healthy soil is about forty-five percent minerals, five percent organic matter, twenty-five percent water and twenty-five percent air.

earth/water-cycle.b23887ccae66: drop the temperature below zero degrees Celsius to see snowfall and snowpack grow. Snowpack is ice storage. Then use the live water counts under the stage to discuss which reservoir is biggest and where water stays longest.
earth/water-cycle.2c4b7956c7f1: A large oak tree can transpire about one hundred fifty thousand liters of water in a year, about forty thousand gallons.
earth/water-cycle.3f6645c4bf16: Water temperature equals the Temperature slider on the three D stage. The sunlight slider also changes how fast the three D ocean evaporates.
earth/water-cycle.a4b11dde42d1: Supports GSE S six E three: the significant role of water in Earth processes, including where water is found on Earth and a model of the water cycle powered by the Sun’s energy and gravity. Water is found in oceans, glaciers, lakes, rivers, groundwater, and the atmosphere. Suggested use: switch the Sun off and have students notice that evaporation nearly stops and clouds fade;
earth/water-cycle.daa27778143c: Transpiration. Plants give off water vapor from their leaves. Roots take up water from the soil. It travels up the stem and escapes through tiny leaf pores called stomata. A large oak tree can transpire about one hundred fifty thousand liters of water in a year, or about forty thousand gallons. About ten percent of the water vapor in the air comes from plants.
earth/water-cycle.39ba82e4c45b: Snow and glaciers. Water stored as ice. When it is cold, precipitation falls as snow and can pile up for years as glaciers and ice caps. Ice caps and glaciers hold about sixty-nine percent of Earth’s fresh water. In spring, snowmelt feeds rivers. Ice can also turn straight into vapor, sublimation. Lower the temperature and watch the snowcap grow!
earth/water-cycle.e79cb7df19da: About eighty-six percent of all evaporation comes from the oceans.
earth/water-cycle.f0fbcec326fc: Typical stay: about three thousand years on average
earth/water-cycle.5358f3697d72: The real thing. The Wabash River winding across its floodplain at Grayville, Illinois. Rivers collect runoff and carry it back toward the sea. Grayville, Illinois, USA
earth/water-cycle.ca20ff4ceb94: You are a drop of water! Choose where to go next, discover which process moves you, and find out how long water usually stays in each place. Can you visit all seven places?
earth/water-cycle.19426ad54a67: The real thing. Heavy rain falling on the Murrumbidgee River in Australia. Precipitation puts water back on the land and into rivers. Wagga Wagga, Australia
earth/water-cycle.e9eca1ad0285: Groundwater is about thirty percent of Earth’s fresh water.
earth/water-cycle.ccbf3b051b43: If all of Earth’s water fit in a one-liter bottle…
earth/water-cycle.4f96e53b09d4: Ice caps and glaciers hold about sixty-nine percent of Earth’s fresh water.
earth/water-cycle.06cdc5a1f072: Memory hint: “ninety-seven salty, three fresh, and most of the fresh is frozen”: about ninety-seven percent of water is salt water, about three percent is fresh, and about two-thirds of that fresh water is ice.
earth/water-cycle.c00923b8e2a2: The real thing. Cumulus clouds. A cloud is not water vapor—that is invisible. It is billions of tiny liquid droplets that condensed out of rising, cooling air.
earth/water-cycle.599ab70e75ca: Surface and other fresh water, one point two percent of fresh water
earth/water-cycle.ed76fb4933af: The real thing. Mist over the rainforest in the Ecuadorian Amazon, near Tena. Rainforest trees release huge amounts of water vapor through their leaves, transpiration, which helps make the clouds and rain. Napo, Ecuador
earth/water-cycle.1dae19b62f6d: Only about three percent is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice caps and glaciers.
earth/water-cycle.c76f88b83040: About ten percent of the water vapor in the air comes from plants.
earth/water-cycle.2f71f6d7ff77: The real thing. The Perito Moreno Glacier in Argentina. Snow that fell long ago is stored here as ice before it finally melts and flows on. Los Glaciares National Park, Argentina
earth/water-cycle.f3d59c3c85a4: The real thing. Water gushing up from the three outlets of Baotu Spring in Jinan, Shandong, China. This is groundwater: rain soaked into the limestone hills south of the city, flowed underground, and comes back up to the surface here. Jinan, Shandong, China
earth/water-cycle.af86c8dc5e0b: Groundwater. Water stored in soil and rock underground. Water that sinks deep fills the pores and cracks in rock. The top of this soaked, saturated, zone is the water table. A rock layer that holds water and lets it flow is an aquifer. Wells pump water from aquifers. Groundwater moves very slowly, often centimeters to meters a day, and eventually seeps into rivers, lakes and the ocean. Groundwater is about thirty percent of Earth’s fresh water.
earth/water-cycle.991cfbf3ff20: Evaporation. Liquid water, water vapor, a gas. Heat from the Sun turns liquid water into invisible water vapor. About eighty-six percent of all evaporation comes from the oceans. When seawater evaporates, the salt stays behind, so the water vapor is fresh. Warmer temperatures mean faster evaporation: try the temperature slider.

earth/weather.9815a8df398d: Warm ocean water. The hurricane’s fuel. Hurricanes need ocean water of at least about twenty-six point five degrees Celsius. Warm water evaporates, loading the air with water vapor. When that vapor condenses into clouds, it releases huge amounts of heat energy. Over land or cold water the fuel is cut off and the storm weakens. Try the ocean-temperature slider!

earth/weather.770d75a928f8: Cumulonimbus. Thunderstorm cloud. A giant tower cloud that can reach twelve kilometers or higher, with a flat anvil top where it hits the stratosphere. Strong updrafts of warm, moist air feed it. It brings lightning, thunder, downpours, hail and sometimes tornadoes. “Cumulus” means heap, and “nimbus” means rain cloud.

Air sinks gently in the eye, so it is surprisingly calm, with light winds and sometimes blue sky. Danger: after the eye passes, the other side of the eyewall hits with winds from the opposite direction.

earth/weathering-erosion.888508657ea3: The real thing. Sand dunes of Erg Chebbi in the Sahara at sunset. Wind piles up loose sand and slowly moves whole dunes. Morocco
earth/weathering-erosion.ec5cb5636ab6: V-shaped valley and canyon. Carved by a river cutting downward. As a river cuts down, weathering and gravity wear back the walls, giving a V shape. The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon over about five to six million years; it is about one point eight kilometers deep, and its walls show layers of rock. Georgia’s Providence Canyon, “Little Grand Canyon”, formed in only about two hundred years, after poor farming in the eighteen hundreds let rain wash gullies into the soft soil — a human impact.
earth/weathering-erosion.6d387b670195: Glacier. A slow river of ice. Glaciers form where more snow falls each winter than melts each summer; the snow packs into ice. The ice slowly flows downhill, often a few centimeters to a meter per day. Rocks frozen into the bottom scrape and grind the bedrock, leaving scratches called striations. About twenty thousand years ago, ice sheets covered much of northern North America, but not Georgia.
earth/weathering-erosion.6c27e6727fda: The real thing. A mushroom-shaped rock in Egypt’s White Desert, where wind erosion has shaped the white chalk into strange forms. White Desert, Egypt

economics/econ-systems.e6243d5c3c41: Command, planned, economy. The central government decides. What to produce? Whatever the government plan sets. How to produce? Planners assign factories, workers and quotas. For whom? The government decides who gets what, often rations. The government owns or controls most land, factories and resources. Strength: it can move huge resources fast toward a goal, heavy industry, dams, railways. Weakness: planners can’t know what millions of people want — shortages and waste are common, and there is little incentive to innovate. Examples: the Soviet Union, nineteen twenty-eight to nineteen ninety-one; North Korea and Cuba today come closest.

economics/econ-systems.4332f74a0417: Mixed economy. Every real country mixes market and government decisions. What to produce? Mostly markets, plus some government choices. How to produce? Private firms and state firms, with rules. For whom? By prices, plus taxes and public services. China calls its system a socialist market economy: public ownership as the mainstay, many forms of ownership developing together, the market playing the decisive role in allocating resources and the government playing its role better. ela/argument-writing.250716a6fed9: Claim. What you want the reader to believe or do. A claim is arguable: a reasonable person could disagree. “School starts at seven forty-five” is a fact, not a claim. Make it specific: who should do what? “Our school should add a twenty-minute recess” beats “Recess is good.” Strong claims often include a reason: “…because students focus better after a break.” Starters: “Our school should…”, “It is time to…”, “The best solution is…”. Claim equals what I think and why, in one sentence. A topic, “phones in school”, is not a claim. A claim takes a side.

ela/argument-writing.4556eed6d41d: Evidence. Facts, data, examples or expert words that support the claim. Strong evidence is specific, numbers, names, dates, reliable, an expert or careful study, and relevant, it really is about your claim. Weak evidence: one person’s story, an unnamed website, or data that is too old for the question. Introduce it: “According to the CDC, …”, “A twenty eighteen study found that…”. Two pieces of strong evidence beat five weak ones. Specific, Reliable, Relevant: S R R. A strong feeling is not evidence. “I really, really believe it” proves nothing.

ela/grammar-sentences.4fd4f993dca5: Fragments and run-ons. The two most common sentence errors. Fragment: missing a subject or verb, or just a dependent clause. Fix: attach it to a sentence. Run-on, fused: “The bus was late we missed the bell.” Comma splice: “The bus was late, we missed the bell.” Fix a run-on four ways: period, semicolon, comma and FANBOYS, or make one clause dependent. Fragment equals too little. Run-on equals too much, no glue. Long is not equal to run-on. A long sentence that’s properly joined is fine.

ela/grammar-sentences.79f2eb7f3e96: Phrase versus clause. A clause has a subject AND a verb; a phrase doesn’t. Phrase: “after the game”, “my little brother”: no subject and verb pair. Clause: “my brother cheered”: subject, brother, and verb, cheered. Independent clause: makes sense alone. Dependent clause: starts with a word like because, when, although, if, until and needs an independent clause. Clause equals who and does what. “Because I was tired.” has a subject and verb but is still a fragment: “because” makes it dependent.

ela/grammar-sentences.4e228bf11f65: Simple sentence. One independent clause. “The storm knocked out the power.” Simple doesn’t mean short: “My little brother and I searched the dark kitchen for candles and matches.” is still simple. ela/narrative-writing.ec0245ed27e8: Conflict. Someone wants something, and something stands in the way. No conflict, no story: “I went to the store and bought milk” is a list, not a story. Types: character versus character, versus nature, versus society, versus self, inner conflict. Raise the stakes: what happens if the character fails? Want and obstacle equals story. Conflict doesn’t have to be a fight. Being scared to sing at the talent show is conflict.

ela/vocabulary-roots.67865813c81b: Latin roots. Everyday school and law words. dict equals say, spect or vis equals see, aud equals hear, port equals carry, rupt equals break, struct equals build, ject equals throw, tract equals pull. Romans spoke Latin; Spanish, French and Italian grew from it, so these roots help with those languages too. About three in ten dictionary words come straight from Latin. Interrupt equals break between. Eject equals throw out. vis and spect both mean “see”: one Latin root can have several forms.

geography/landforms.af491893a7d7: This is the same land seen from straight above. Each brown contour line joins points of the same elevation, and neighboring lines are two hundred meters apart, the contour interval. Drag a line across the map to slice the land and see its cross-section.
geography/landforms.1b76656031b3: A simplified picture based on the Grand Canyon in Arizona: it assumes the Colorado River cut down about one thousand six hundred meters at a steady speed over roughly six million years, a depth of one mile. Dates and speeds are approximate.
geography/landforms.e95191d468a1: Memory hint: Mountains equals high, steep and peaks. On a contour map, their lines are packed tightly together.
geography/landforms.08f483fffe6c: Lake. Water surrounded by land. A lake is a body of water surrounded by land. Most lakes are fresh water. Lakes fill low places: hollows dug by glaciers, cracks in the crust, old volcano craters, or dams. A reservoir is a human-made lake behind a dam, like Lake Lanier in Georgia. Great Lakes, USA and Canada. Lake Baikal, deepest. Lake Victoria, Africa. Caspian Sea, largest, salty.
geography/landforms.503d489ee2fb: Mountains. High land with steep sides and peaks. Mountains rise steeply far above the land around them. A long chain of mountains is a mountain range. Most big ranges form where tectonic plates collide and push rock upward, the Himalayas, or where volcanoes erupt. It gets colder as you climb, so high peaks can stay snow-covered all year. Himalayas, Mount Everest, eight thousand eight hundred forty-nine meters. Andes, Rocky Mountains, Alps, Blue Ridge Mountains in north Georgia.
geography/landforms.46708c7a122c: A contour map has a two hundred meter interval. Starting at sea level, you walk uphill and cross four contour lines. About how high are you?
geography/landforms.5371e48d9578: Peninsula: land poking into water, water on three sides. Gulf: water poking into land, land on three sides.
geography/landforms.5796c9d0f0e5: The name comes from the Greek letter delta, capital delta, a triangle.
geography/landforms.48a25d4a3be5: Memory hint: Elevation is measured from sea level, zero meters.
geography/landforms.f7b065e160a2: Plateau. High land that is flat on top. A plateau is a large area of high, fairly flat land with at least one steep side, like a giant table, it is also called a tableland. The Tibetan Plateau averages about four thousand five hundred meters high and is nicknamed the “Roof of the World”. Rivers often cut deep canyons into plateaus, like the Colorado River in the Colorado Plateau. Tibetan Plateau, Colorado Plateau, Deccan Plateau, India, Mexican Plateau, Brazilian Highlands.
geography/landforms.0a526865b66b: Ideas: one, Play the River journey story and ask whether the river is eroding or depositing at each step. two, Raise sea level by one hundred fifty meters and ask which landforms flood first and why delta cities worry most about rising seas. three, Turn on Contour lines and find the same plateau in both the three D model and the topographic map. four, Have students drag a cross-section through the canyon and describe its shape.
geography/landforms.78360101f043: Memory hint: delta delta equals a triangle of mud at the river’s mouth.
geography/landforms.0f4a66e25d77: Running water slowly wore the rock away, cutting down about one point eight kilometers.
geography/landforms.d9fd0bc5a2c8: Lake Baikal. The deepest lake on Earth and the oldest, about twenty-five million years old, in Siberia, Russia. It is one thousand six hundred forty-two meters deep. It holds more fresh water than all five Great Lakes together.
geography/landforms.5b4665b0a741: Canyon. A deep, narrow valley with cliff walls. A canyon, or gorge, is a very deep, narrow valley with steep, cliff-like sides. Most canyons are carved by a river cutting down through rock over millions of years, erosion. The walls show layers of rock. The deeper the layer, the older it usually is. Grand Canyon, about one point eight kilometers deep, carved by the Colorado River. Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon, Tibet. Tallulah Gorge, Georgia.
geography/landforms.e2960d6f9bae: Greenland. The world’s largest island, about two point two million square kilometers, mostly buried under an ice sheet up to three kilometers thick. Only about fifty-seven thousand people live there, on the coast.
geography/landforms.57afcabd2397: Oceans are the largest bodies of salt water. They cover about seventy-one percent of Earth’s surface.
geography/landforms.d57f7aa64a52: Supports the Georgia Social Studies standards S S six G and S S seven G, for example, S S six G one, S S six G eight, S S six G one one, S S seven G one, S S seven G five, S S seven G eight: locate major physical features of each region, such as the Andes, the Amazon River, the Iberian Peninsula, the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Himalayas, plus the map and globe skills of reading contour lines, scale and a compass rose. This page builds the vocabulary first.
geography/landforms.a3edd578cf23: How can a river carve a canyon a mile deep? Earth’s surface is anything but flat: towering mountains, flat plateaus and plains, plus rivers, lakes, gulfs and straits. Spin the three D diorama below, click anywhere to name what you see, then follow a river all the way from the mountains to the sea!
geography/landforms.f70303c70b74: Ocean and coast. The huge salty water around the continents. Oceans are the largest bodies of salt water. They cover about seventy-one percent of Earth’s surface. There are five oceans: Pacific, largest, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. The coast is where land meets the sea. Move the sea-level slider to see how coastlines change. Pacific Ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Georgia’s coast, Indian Ocean, Mediterranean Sea, Caribbean Sea.
geography/landforms.ec02a9049560: Delta. New land built at a river’s mouth. When a river reaches the sea it slows down and drops its sediment. Over time this builds a fan- or triangle-shaped delta. The name comes from the Greek letter delta, capital delta, a triangle. Delta soil is very fertile, so deltas are crowded with farms and people, but they flood easily. Nile Delta, Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, largest, Mississippi Delta, Yangtze River Delta, Pearl River Delta.

Also: some maps split the Eastern and Western Hemispheres at twenty degrees west and one hundred sixty degrees east so that Africa and Europe are not cut in half. This includes maps in Chinese textbooks. US classes usually use the prime meridian and the one hundred eighty degree meridian.

geography/latitude-longitude.8998635e2446: Latitude, parallels. How far NORTH or SOUTH of the equator. Lines of latitude circle Earth east-west, but they measure distance north or south. They never meet, so they are also called parallels. Latitude runs from zero degrees at the equator to ninety degrees north at the North Pole and ninety degrees south at the South Pole. One degree of latitude is always about one hundred eleven kilometers, sixty-nine miles. Parallels get shorter toward the poles; each pole is just a point.

geography/world-religions.316383a266f1: Judaism: by tradition, Abraham traveled from Ur to Canaan about eighteen hundred B C E. Judaism teaches belief in one God. The Torah is its holiest text.
geography/world-religions.a1c3da60c351: The Four Noble Truths: there is suffering, craving gives rise to it, suffering can end, and the Eightfold Path leads to its end. The Middle Way: avoiding both indulgence and extreme self-denial. Karma and rebirth; the goal is nirvana, freedom from suffering and rebirth
geography/world-religions.34f2b99cc6b9: Three world religions in the textbook. Grade nine World History covers Buddhism, Christianity and Islam. For Buddhism, it covers ancient India and Siddhartha Gautama. For Christianity, it covers the first century C E, Roman-ruled Palestine and Jesus. For Islam, it covers the early seventh century C E, the Arabian Peninsula and Muhammad. The textbook traditionally places the founding of Buddhism in the sixth century B C E.

Xi’an’s Big Wild Goose Pagoda was built to house Buddhist texts and other items from his journey.

Key texts: The Torah, first five books of the Hebrew Bible, Tanakh; the Talmud records rabbinic discussions of Jewish law and tradition. One God, who made a covenant, a special agreement, with Abraham and his descendants. Follow God’s laws, including the Ten Commandments. Keep the Sabbath: a weekly day of rest from Friday evening until Saturday nightfall

Martin Luther King Jr. was born at five oh one Auburn Avenue in nineteen twenty-nine and preached at Ebenezer Baptist Church with his father. The SCLC was founded here in nineteen fifty-seven; SNCC made Atlanta its headquarters in October nineteen sixty. College students began the Atlanta Student Movement in nineteen sixty with “An Appeal for Human Rights” and lunch-counter sit-ins. Dr. Thomas Brewer recruited Primus King to try to vote in the July fourth, nineteen forty-four, Democratic primary. King was turned away. His lawsuit, King versus Chapman, struck down Georgia’s whites-only primary in nineteen forty-five; the ruling was upheld in nineteen forty-six. In one-party Georgia the Democratic primary decided who won, so this opened real voting power. Black voter registration jumped to about one hundred twenty-five thousand within months.

georgia/ga-geography.4ad467ffcbaa: Brasstown Bald. Four thousand seven hundred eighty-four feet, one thousand four hundred fifty-eight meters — the roof of Georgia. On a clear day you can see four states from the tower on top: Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina and South Carolina.

georgia/ga-geography.6043985121e4: Blue Ridge. Georgia’s tallest mountains. Location: the northeast corner. Brasstown Bald is the highest point in Georgia, at four thousand seven hundred eighty-four feet or one thousand four hundred fifty-eight meters; the Appalachian Trail starts at Springer Mountain. Climate: the coolest region, with some snow in winter and the most rain in the state — up to about seventy to eighty inches a year. Agriculture: apples in Ellijay, cattle, poultry and hardwood forests on steep slopes. Economy: tourism and timber — and the eighteen twenty-nine gold rush at Dahlonega. Tourism includes hiking, rafting and Tallulah Gorge.
georgia/ga-geography.d3ffe896aa78: Chattahoochee River. Atlanta’s water supply and part of the Alabama border. About four hundred thirty miles from the Blue Ridge to the Florida line. Lake Lanier stores its water for metro Atlanta; Columbus grew at its Fall Line falls; it forms much of the Georgia-Alabama border.

georgia/ga-geography.7bfdfb8a6f54: Piedmont. Rolling hills and red clay. Location: from the mountains down to the Fall Line — about a third of Georgia. “Piedmont” means “foot of the mountains.” Climate: hot summers, mild winters, about fifty inches of rain. Rolling hills of red clay, colored by iron, and granite such as Stone Mountain. Agriculture: poultry, Gainesville calls itself the “Poultry Capital of the World”, cattle, dairy, timber; it was cotton country in the eighteen hundreds. Economy: the most people and jobs — Atlanta, Athens and the busy Hartsfield-Jackson airport; business, transportation, government and universities.

georgia/ga-geography.ec100f0bd6b4: Atlanta isn’t on a big river. Most of its water comes from the Chattahoochee and Lake Lanier, made by Buford Dam in the nineteen fifties. In dry years Georgia, Alabama and Florida have argued for decades over sharing that water — the “tri-state water wars.”
georgia/ga-geography.15628637370d: Two hundred years ago there were no railroads — goods moved by boat. Paddle upriver from the coast and you hit a “step”: the Fall Line, where the hard rock of the Piedmont meets the soft sand and clay of the Coastal Plain. Rapids and waterfalls stop the boats. georgia/ga-geography.9340b8623abf: Tallulah Gorge. A gorge almost one thousand feet deep. The Tallulah River cut this gorge about two miles long. In nineteen seventy Karl Wallenda walked across it on a tightrope.

georgia/ga-geography.fc6c952e4263: Georgia has a humid subtropical climate: hot, sticky summers and mild winters. But the higher and farther north you go, the cooler it gets — a January day averages about thirty-seven degrees Fahrenheit in the mountains, or three degrees Celsius, and about fifty degrees Fahrenheit in Savannah, or ten degrees Celsius. The south also has a longer growing season, which is why the Coastal Plain became the big farming region.
georgia/ga-geography.a3fc81d1674b: Valley and Ridge. Ridges and fertile valleys side by side. Location: the northwest, between the Appalachian Plateau and the Blue Ridge. Long ridges such as Taylor Ridge run southwest to northeast with valleys between. Climate: mild — cooler than the south, with about fifty to fifty-five inches of rain. Agriculture: grain, hay, cattle, poultry and dairy in the limestone valleys. Economy: manufacturing — Dalton is called the “Carpet Capital of the World”; Rome grew where two rivers meet to form the Coosa.
georgia/ga-geography.47f524c82028: Most of Georgia gets about forty-five to fifty-five inches of rain a year, one thousand one hundred to one thousand four hundred millimeters. The northeast mountains catch moist air and get the most — up to about seventy to eighty inches. Summer thunderstorms, hurricanes in late summer and fall, and occasional droughts all affect farming and water supply.
georgia/ga-geography.50b604e98cab: Four thousand seven hundred eighty-four minus one thousand fifty, about three thousand seven hundred feet — more than two and a half Empire State Buildings stacked up.
georgia/ga-geography.682c0701484e: Appalachian Mountains, Springer Mountain. The southern end of a one thousand five hundred-mile mountain chain. The Appalachians cover the Blue Ridge, Valley and Ridge and Appalachian Plateau. Mountains block easy travel, so north Georgia was settled later — and its rain feeds rivers for the whole state.
georgia/ga-geography.ec6e7ec451df: Savannah, near the mouth of the Savannah River, has been a port since seventeen thirty-three; today it is one of the busiest container ports in the US. Brunswick ships huge numbers of cars. Before railroads, Fall Line cities marked the end of river travel.

georgia/ga-government.b9e5c71e3f30: The Governor. Carries out and enforces the laws. Governor: at least thirty, a US citizen for fifteen years and a Georgia resident for six years. A four-year term, at most two terms in a row. The lieutenant governor has the same qualifications, presides over the Senate and becomes governor if the office is empty. The governor writes the budget proposal, sets the revenue estimate, signs or vetoes bills and can veto single spending items. Other statewide elected officers include the secretary of state, attorney general, state school superintendent and agriculture commissioner. State agencies do the daily work: Department of Education, Department of Transportation, GDOT, Department of Driver Services, your license, Department of Natural Resources, state parks, Department of Juvenile Justice.

georgia/ga-government.bf81e563954d: The current constitution took effect on the first of July, nineteen eighty-three — Georgia’s tenth, seventeen seventy-seven, seventeen eighty-nine, seventeen ninety-eight, eighteen sixty-one, eighteen sixty-five, eighteen sixty-eight, eighteen seventy-seven, nineteen forty-five, nineteen seventy-six, nineteen eighty-three. It opens with a preamble; Article One is the Bill of Rights; there are eleven articles in all. Like the US Constitution it sets up three branches and protects rights — but the US Constitution is the supreme law, so Georgia’s may not conflict with it.

georgia/ga-government.22c69b29c466: General Assembly. Makes the laws and passes the budget. Two chambers: the Senate, fifty-six senators, and the House of Representatives, one hundred eighty representatives. All serve two-year terms. Qualifications: senators at least twenty-five, representatives at least twenty-one; US citizens; Georgia residents for two years and district residents for one year. Meets every year from the second Monday in January for forty legislative days — usually into late March or early April. Leaders: the lieutenant governor presides over the Senate; the House elects its own Speaker. Committees study every bill first — most bills never leave committee. Committees include Education, Appropriations, Judiciary… Spending and tax bills must start in the House.

georgia/ga-government.6d819ca357a1: The Courts. Interprets the laws and administers justice. Supreme Court: nine justices — the highest court; it decides questions about the constitution and reviews the most serious cases. Court of Appeals: fifteen judges who check trial courts for legal mistakes. Trial courts: superior, felonies, divorce, land. State. Juvenile. Probate, wills, marriage licenses. And magistrate, warrants, small claims. Judges are chosen in nonpartisan elections — no party label on the ballot. When a seat opens early, the governor appoints a judge. Dual purpose: interpret what the laws mean, and administer justice by deciding cases fairly.

georgia/ga-modern.8ac36d54264b: Film studios, Fayetteville. Sound stages south of Atlanta. In two thousand eight Georgia began offering film and TV companies a tax credit of up to thirty percent of what they spend in the state. Big studio campuses grew up around Atlanta, such as Trilith Studios in Fayetteville and Tyler Perry Studios on the old Fort McPherson army base. Direct spending hit a record of about four point four billion dollars in fiscal twenty twenty-two, then fell to two point six billion dollars in fiscal twenty twenty-four after Hollywood strikes.
georgia/ga-modern.680740b25fc6: In nineteen seventy-three, at thirty-five, Jackson was elected mayor of Atlanta, taking office in nineteen seventy-four — the first Black mayor of a major Southern city. He insisted that minority-owned firms get a fair share of city contracts — up from under one percent to more than thirty-five percent — and oversaw a huge new airport terminal, finished ahead of schedule and under budget. He won a third term in nineteen ninety.
georgia/ga-modern.f0f191b5e812: Port of Brunswick. America’s busiest port for autos and heavy machinery. Ships here are “roll-on and roll-off”: cars, tractors and bulldozers drive on and off. In twenty twenty-four and again in twenty twenty-five the Georgia Ports Authority reported Brunswick as the nation’s busiest port for autos and heavy equipment. Twenty twenty-five: about seven hundred seventy-nine thousand autos plus more than fifty-three thousand units of heavy machinery.
georgia/ga-modern.42924533ff56: Downtown Atlanta. Where the nineteen ninety-six Games and two mayors reshaped a city. Maynard Jackson and Andrew Young helped turn Atlanta into an international city. Maynard Jackson was mayor from nineteen seventy-four, and Andrew Young from nineteen eighty-two to nineteen ninety. Centennial Olympic Park, built for nineteen ninety-six on run-down land, is now ringed by attractions such as the Georgia Aquarium, the World of Coca-Cola and the National Center for Civil and Human Rights — tourism in action. The Carter Center, founded by Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter in nineteen eighty-two, is a few miles east.

georgia/ga-modern.91c09361478f: Port of Savannah. Georgia’s doorway to world trade. Garden City Terminal handles containers — standard steel boxes measured in TEU. One twenty-foot box equals one TEU. The channel was deepened from forty-two to forty-seven feet so bigger ships can come in more fully loaded. The deepening took place from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-two. Fiscal twenty twenty-one: five point three million TEU — the first Southeast or Gulf port over five million. Record: five point seven six million in fiscal twenty twenty-two.

The company aims for about eight thousand five hundred jobs at the plant by twenty thirty-one, plus thousands more at suppliers. It sits close to the Port of Savannah — handy for parts coming in and cars going out.
